maintopic: OIL-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REMOVAL OF U.S. RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN IMPORTS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: OIL-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REMOVAL OF U.S. RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the house knows, the United States since July of 1957 has restricted imports of oil, first by what was known as the voluntary oil imports program and, since March 10, 1959, by mandatory controls. This government has consistently maintained and repeatedly emphasized to the government of the United States that we could not recognize that such controls were consistent with the mutual security interest of Canada and the United States and with the economic co-operation which must underlie such a vital common interest.
I am pleased, therefore to be able to tell the house that the United States government has today announced the exemption from import restrictions of crude oil, unfinished oils, and finished petroleum products which enter the United States by pipe line, motor carrier or rail from the country in which they are produced. Under the terms of the United States government decision the exemption will become effective as of June 1 next.
I wish to take this occasion to express the Canadian government's satisfaction at the decision which has been taken and announced by the United States. I am glad to recognize that it is the consequence of a desire on the part of the United States administration to reach agreement with Canada in the solution of a difficult problem.
The exemption will be of direct benefit to the export sales of Canadian crude oil and products. As important, if not more, is the benefit which will follow in terms of a normal, healthy development of the Canadian petroleum industry, which is thus restored to its appropriate place as an important and natural supplier of the North American markets.
In addition to its intrinsic importance for the future of the Canadian oil industry, the decision is also of significance in terms of our general relations with the United States in that it removes a source of distressing irritation and reflects a degree of co-operation and sensible development of resources which is so necessary for the economic prosperity and mutual defence of our two countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: OIL-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REMOVAL OF U.S. RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house will have heard with great satisfaction from the Prime Minister of the decision of the United States government to lift the restriction on the export from Canada to the United States of this very important product. We all hope this may be followed by an increase in our exports of oil to the United States and in an encouragement to the development of this industry.
Perhaps I am not right in this assumption, but I assume from the Prime Minister's statement that the action taken by the government of the United States affects Canadian oil and not imports of oil from other countries in this hemisphere. If that assumption is correct perhaps I may be permitted to ask the Prime Minister whether as a result of the discussions and negotiations that have been carried on in Washington, Canada's hands are tied in any way in regard to any action which we may feel obliged to take in the future concerning imports of oil from, say, Venezuela.

maintopic: OIL-ANNOUNCEMENT OF REMOVAL OF U.S. RESTRICTIONS ON CERTAIN IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement by the Prime Minister is a welcome one. I believe that parliament as a whole has supported the representations the government of Canada has made to the United States. We have supported the government in these actions, and we are fully confident of the fact that because parliament spoke with one voice this had some bearing on the important results announced today.
This announcement is of importance to the Canadian oil industry and to the oil industry of western Canada in particular. In recent months there have been serious cut-backs in production. There has been a reluctance on the part of oil companies to continue exploration at a rapid pace. We hope this will restore morale to the oil industry and mean an expanded exploration and development program. We believe it should result in increased markets for Canadian oil.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 11, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Fleming (Eglinton)-Mr. Rea in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to extend for a further period of one year the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we last had this resolution before us on March 11, in the dying minutes of the day the minister made an appeal to the house, as recorded on page 1854 of Hansard, to agree to the passing of this resolution. At the time I indicated we were not yet prepared to allow the resolution to pass so the minister might introduce the bill, because looking at the wording of the resolution it is obvious that once the bill is before us we will be limited very much indeed in our debate on the matter. Once the bill is before us we will be limited to the terms which are outlined in the bill. Looking at the resolution, it says:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act-
There is a feeling in our group that the word "expedient" in this context is of importance. I looked up the word in the dictionary, and I found that "expedient" may 

mean that "it is advisable". However, I also noticed in one dictionary that in the days of William Shakespeare the word "expedient" could be interpreted as "hasty". I believe that the Elizabethan interpretation of the word "expedient" ought to apply here. I would prefer to say that the resolution ought to read: "Resolved that because of the lack of policy and the unwillingness to fulfil election pledges, it is regrettable that it is expedient that this measure now be introduced."
I realize that a ruling has been given that we may not at this time debate the advisability of calling together a formal dominion-provincial conference. The minister has indicated that there is to be a meeting of the finance ministers of the ten provincial governments himself, and to that end the minister has indicated on the orders of the day that he has now employed a roving ambassador who is interviewing the ten provincial finance ministers.
I hope that before the resolution is adopted the minister is going to indicate to the house what kind of reception this roving ambassador has received and when we may expect the meeting of the finance ministers. We feel that the government has ignored its election pledges, that it is carrying on the old policy, and that it is employing an ad hoc philosophy in regard to the financial resources of the various levels of government. We in our group feel that there ought to be developing in Canada the idea that the federal government should begin to share the responsibilities that are faced by various levels of government in the year 1959. We prefer a sharing of responsibilities attitude to the approach that used to be expounded by the Conservatives when in opposition, which was one of the federal government relinquishing certain sources of revenue in favour of other levels of government.
We should like to ask the minister this question. On what basis is this resolution founded? Why does he ask the house to continue the old arrangement? I have indicated before that what the minister is now asking is not in line with his election speeches. We notice-and it is with agreement on our part-that the government has provided for extraordinary grants for a number of our Canadian provinces, namely Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. We notice also, and with extreme pleasure, that the federal government under the auspices of the Prime Minister has at long last agreed to share the cost of a major undertaking in the province of Saskatchewan. I refer, of course, to the building of the dam. We also note with some agreement that the federal government is willing to share responsibility in the field

of unemployment by way of its winter works program, that the federal government has also agreed to help in the development of natural resources, and has itself evolved a roads to resources program. We hear-and we hear this only by way of the "grapevine" -that the federal government is about to undertake a sharing of some responsibilities with the government of Manitoba, and we hope an announcement in that regard will not be very long delayed.
This problem which faces our ten provincial governments and all our municipal governments is a very serious one. Since March 11, when this question was last under discussion, we have received information regarding the expected revenues and expenditures of each of our provincial governments. We have also read a good deal in our home town newspapers about the budgets of our municipal governments. It causes us a great deal of concern when we realize that our municipal governments, almost without exception, have found it necessary to raise the mill rate.
I know the advice the Prime Minister gave to the municipalities last October was that if they did not wish to raise their mill rates, maybe they ought to raise their assessments. That is advice which I think could be exploded by any 14 or 15-year old in Canada. However, we regret that our municipalities, by reason of the niggardliness of this federal government, are in the position where they must either raise their mill rates or their assessments. I may say that many municipalities and provinces are giving very serious consideration to the imposition of a retail sales tax in order that they may be able to meet their obligations. I understand that in the province of Manitoba, unless there is an extraordinary announcement on the part of the national government, a sales tax will be imposed after May 14.
I should like at this point to read the receipts by way of taxation for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957. I notice that the federal government received the sum of $5,019 million. Our provinces were able to collect $733 million, and our municipal governments were able to raise the sum of $923 million. In other words, of all the taxes levied upon Canadians 75 per cent went to the Minister of Finance here in Ottawa, our ten ministers of finance in the provinces collected 11 per cent, and our municipalities collected 14 per cent.
Now let us look at what happened in the year 1937. We see that in that year the federal government did not receive 75 per cent of the taxes the Canadian people had to pay. They received only 47 per cent. Our provincial governments did not receive 11 per

I wish it were possible, Mr. Chairman, and I think it would be profitable, for those in this house to have an honest, heart to heart and down to earth conversation on the entire question of federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements. I think it would be for the good of Canada if that could be done without reference to points of order, previous decisions and precedents. In my opinion one of the most difficult problems facing the various governments of our country today is that of having sufficient revenue, from old or new sources, to meet the new and varying responsibilities with which they are faced.
I am firmly of the belief that the provinces and municipalities have a very good case in asking for a reasonable and logical basis for the sharing of taxation. I had the privilege, Mr. Chairman, of being the leader of the opposition in British Columbia when the first tax-sharing arrangement was made between the federal government and the provinces of Canada. I can well remember the thinking in the British Columbia legislature at that time. What was noted then I think should be noted here this afternoon, when we are discussing the resolution now before us.
There can be no question but that the provinces, under the British North America Act, were given and still have the right of direct taxation. It was the provinces which exercised that right in the first instance by the introduction of the income tax, corporation tax and succession duties. Because of the exigencies of world war I Sir Robert Borden, then prime minister, moved the federal government into the field of direct taxation under the over-all section of the British North America Act.
To the best of my knowledge there was an indication given at that time by the federal government under Sir Robert Borden that this move of the federal government in the field of direct taxation was made only because of the exigencies of war and there was no intention of remaining in that which was accepted as being a provincial tax field.
3192	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations However, the federal government having got its foot in the door of the provincial field of taxation never got its foot out. It has not only stayed in continuously and consistently, but in 1941 it got more than a foot in the door; it shoved all the way in when, because of the exigencies of another world war, it introduced an arrangement between the federal and provincial governments whereby the tax was levied by one government only but there was a sharing by two.
I fully realize that in the original introduction of this method in 1941 it was understood, and I think it still is, that a basis was provided upon which a province may withdraw; but I know that the majority of the provinces of Canada realize that people do not like being taxed twice or having to fill out two forms if one will do the job. Therefore the federal government is in a very strong position in that regard. Mr. Chairman, I honestly believe that the federal government when it considers, as it is now considering, a continuation for a further year of the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements it has more than a moral responsibility in this matter. In fact, the federal government is an interloper in this field of taxation, although under one general clause they have the right of so taxing. I admit that never will the federal government be able to remove itself from that field of taxation; but I do think there is a moral responsibility to remember the statements made by Sir Robert Borden back in the time of the first world war that it was only a temporary measure; and remember too the arguments used to the provinces in 1941 as to why they should give up their rights of taxation in the direct field and operate jointly with the federal government.
There is also something which is perhaps of more paramount importance than that, and that is that when the fathers of confederation drafted the British North America Act, brilliant as they were, and brilliant as is the document which became the constitution of Canada, they could not have anticipated or foreseen the economy of Canada or the new responsibilities of government for the next hundred years. I feel that all members of this house, whether cabinet ministers or hon. members, are dodging the issue and refusing to face up to facts. We must recognize that in making a federal-provincial tax-sharing agreement it has to be done with an understanding of the new responsibilities of all forms of government and the need for money in order to meet these responsibilities which were not foreseen 100 years ago.

I know there are many who think that the British North America Act is something which is sacrosanct and, like the sacred cows in India, completely untouchable. Mr. Chairman, we are not going to be able to appreciate fully federal-provincial taxation agreements unless we recognize the need now for the clarification of the responsibilities of the three levels of government and how they are going to be able to meet their financial responsibilities. That will in my estimation, in the long run, most definitely require not only understanding between governments but also revision of the British North America Act.
Whether we like to name it as such or not, we are rapidly moving into a welfare state society. Because the allocation of responsibilities, quite understandably, could not have been foreseen 100 years ago, we find today between federal, provincial and municipal levels of government an absolute hodgepodge of security measures and responsibilities which makes it almost impossible for a municipal government, a provincial government or a federal government to know quite where they are going or how to finance themselves.
May I very briefly outline the situation in which the governments find themselves today? If it is a question of workmen's compensation, that is a provincial responsibility. If it is mothers' pensions, that is a provincial responsibility. If it is welfare, the responsibility for that has been changing over the years but now it is a federal, provincial and municipal responsibility. A municipality does not know where it stands because its position is determined by the province. If it is family allowances, that is a federal responsibility. If it is unemployment, that is federal. Unemployment insurance payments are the responsibility of the employer, the employee and the federal government. If it is old age pensions, for the over 70's it is federal, but under 70 it is federal and provincial. Now in our normal and understandable development we have reached a hodgepodge of security measures where the responsibility in one case is provincial, in another dominion and provincial, and in yet another dominion, provincial and municipal.
Surely the point I am trying to make is understandable to all. We have reached the point where we are entering into a welfare state and building up progressively, as we must do, a system of security measures, but on an unrealistic basis. We must understand that what applied 100 years ago does not apply now and there must be found some method or means of allocating responsibility, and with responsibility the ability to pay for those responsibilities. That is something, Mr. Chairman, which I think must be considered


in the very near future by the government of Canada and any provincial government which calls itself a responsible government.
But because that situation has not yet come about and, undoubtedly, it will be some time before it does, we must extend a considerable measure of sincere understanding to the municipalities and to the provinces, because in this coming year they have to rely to a great extent on measures taken by this House of Commons in connection with tax-sharing arrangements. I can understand the unhappiness felt by the provinces in this regard, in the light of the fact that there is to be no change in the basis of tax-sharing in the coming year as compared with the basis of sharing revenues in the past year. The responsibilities of the provinces and of the municipalities are increasing, yet the means open to them for collecting money through taxes continue to be limited as before. The federal government has the broad field of taxation to cover, and is not exercising its prerogative of collecting money from sources where it can be collected, such as racketeers and profiteers. This is an avenue not open to the provincial governments and to the municipalities, and for this reason the dominion government has an even greater responsibility for assisting other levels of government.
It must be remembered, too, that the responsibility for taking the initiative in these matters lies with the federal government. It is the federal government which must do the basic thinking, and initiate the studies which are required if the sharing of taxation revenue in the light of governmental responsibilities is to be placed on a scientific and constitutional basis. This is, in my view, an added reason why the provincial governments are entitled to more consideration than it would appear they are to be given judging from the motion which is now before us. I do not object to being called a politician, because I think that is an honourable word, but I venture to say it is high time that the government showed a little more statesmanship in dealing with this particular subject, since statesmanship is now something which is most needed in Canada.

Mr. Chairman,
the matter of federal-provincial relations is a very important one, it is even a vital matter for our country, for the provinces and also for the municipalities and school boards. In short, it is of vital importance for all Cana-
30, 1959
Dominion-Provincial Relations dian citizens whatever province they come from, because the federal policy in this field with regard to the provinces may affect the entire economy of this country; it will, indeed, have repercussions on the means the provinces, municipalities and school boards have of fulfilling their obligations with regard to the people.
The members of the government now in power, when they were sitting on this side of the house, felt strongly about federal-provincial relations. They also felt strongly on the matter during the 1957 election. Even in 1956, during the national convention of the Conservative party, a manifesto was prepared with regard to practically all matters concerning the federal government, the provinces and municipalities as well as the school boards. But the manifesto was never made public. There had been prepared, so it seems, a press release which was held back. However, this is what we find on page 4 of that manifesto with regard to federal-provincial relations. I quote:
We have full confidence in the federal system of government such as it is outlined in the British North America Act which divides responsibilities and obligations between the federal government and the provinces. That system is jeopardized by the exaggerated centralization practised by the present federal government. In order to restore a just balance between the Dominion and the provinces, we shall ensure;
Then comes a series of steps that are advocated, but I shall read only two. Paragraph (d) reads:
The working out, after consulting with the provinces, of a lasting solution to the problem of fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces.
And paragraph (e) says:
We also are of the opinion that provincial governments and municipal councils should have sufficient financial means to carry out their constitutional responsibilities and meet the ever growing needs for education and public services in order to ensure the constant development of their economic productivity.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, that manifesto never was released. Various reasons were given by some groups, but the fact remains that the public never was informed of the resolutions in this field which had been passed during the convention which elected the present Prime Minister leader of the Conservative party.
There is also the Minister of Finance who spoke very feelingly, when sitting on this side of the house, about federal-provincial relations. My colleague from Hull (Mr. Caron) recalled some of his words. I too
3194	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Dominion-Provincial Relations
should like to recall one in particular, which he said when the house was considering, in 1956, the new money-sharing project with the provinces. It was the project introduced by the hon. Mr. Harris. On page 6287 of Hansard of July 23, 1956, there appears the following, which was spoken at the time by the present Minister of Finance, then member for Eglinton.
The question that we ought to ask ourselves is similar to that which my leader put before the house when he spoke a week ago. To paraphrase it, I would say the question before us is whether or not at this time there is evidence that the proposals of the government, and in particular this formula, will satisfactorily meet the demands which are actually now imposed upon provincial governments, municipal councils and boards of education throughout Canada and particularly whether they will be adequate over the five-year period during which the new scheme is intended to be in effect.
As to the details of the formula, suffice it to say at this point that it is an actuarial maze to most people. The formula itself would undoubtedly confuse most citizens. Talk of tax equalization payments, provincial revenue stabilization payments, tax rental agreements, gross national product, average personal income, and other expressions in which this formula abounds make it very difficult for the average citizen to appreciate the niceties of the formula.
Mr. Chairman, since the Minister of Finance took over his portfolio, he must have had some opportunity of studying the formula, and he must have understood it very well for he has kept using it.
And later on, the hon. member for Eglinton said, as recorded on page 6297 of Hansard of the same date:
Therefore, sir, apart from all other considerations, some of which I have mentioned, I give this house in conclusion ten reasons why, because of its utter inadequacy, we of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, cannot support this bill and why we shall on second reading vote against it.
And do you know what those ten reasons were, Mr. Chairman? When I read that, I was expecting very sound reasons, something really solid; but the hon. member for Eglinton merely said: First, it makes inadequate provision for Prince Edward Island. He then went on to enumerate the nine other provinces, after Prince-Edward Island. Those are rather insignificant and childish reasons to oppose the equalization formula, such as it was introduced in 1956.
During the 1957 campaign, the matter of federal-provincial relations was raised.
I shall not take much of the time of the house, because I only wish to quote two or three promises made at that time, when the former Liberal administration was accused of having treated the provinces with arrogance, of having failed entirely to settle the question of federal-provincial relations,

and of having taken only unilateral action in that regard.
Here is what the Prime Minister said on May 27, 1957, at Saskatoon, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 28, 1957:
(Text):
Any new decision, he added, would be based not on the Liberal policy of a grasping greed for dollars but only on the basis of agreement by all the provinces. "They are all equal", he underlined.
(Translation):
On May 7, 1957 in Hull, according to Le Droit for the next day, the present Prime Minister had this to say:
The Leader of the Opposition said that he has noticed the same uneasiness in all the municipalities of western Quebec, where he met no less than 20 mayors who are all faced with increasingly acute financial problems.
The new Conservative leader pledged that, as soon as his party is elected to power he will call a federal-provincial conference to revamp the tax sharing system between the central government and the provinces and municipalities.
On May 22, 1957, the present Prime Minister made a speech in Victoria-that is he spoke on May 21 but the report was published the next day in the Victoria Times. And this is what he said:
(Text):
The plight of the municipalities is becoming tragic because there is a constant increase in federal taxes. Now the federal government takes the attitude that there is no responsibility on them to assure that the municipalities shall have the right to discharge their responsibilities-
The municipalities find themselves unable to carry on because they are being restricted of the sources of revenue.
The premiers of many provinces, he said, had complained there was no recognition of their fiscal needs.
Even the city of Victoria has to pay outrageous rates of interest today. Taxation is falling more and more on local residents in our municipalities.
The time has come for a meeting of the provinces and the federal government, with the municipalities present, to discuss these problems.
We intend to convene such a meeting in the spirit of confederation. If action is not taken we shall find ourselves in a position in five years' time where the municipalities will be bankrupt or unable to carry out their responsibilities.
(Translation):
I will quote only a few of his promises, because we already have two full books of them and soon we will probably have to make up a third one because there are Conservative members who, at certain by-election campaigns, go out and add to the innumerable promises that were made in 1957 and 1958.
In a speech he made in Massey Hall, in
Toronto, at the start of the 1957 campaign_______
on April 25, 1957 to be more precise-the Prime Minister had this to say:

(Text):
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation; have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue; have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibilities or permitting the necessary development in their own territorial confines of the natural resources that there are. We believe the provinces and municipalities must have the financial resources to carry out those responsibilities. We believe in the federal system of government. We believe that its preservation is essential to Canadian unity. We believe the federal system is today being challenged by the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government and that a healthy division and balance of revenues as between the federal and provincial governments must be assured.
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect. (Translation):
That is the kind of statements and promises made to the nation by the Prime Minister, both as leader of the opposition and in 1958, after he had become Prime Minister of this country.
I do not suppose we can discuss federal provincial relations without being allowed at the same time to discuss the matter of a federal-provincial conference. If opposition members are refused a chance to deal with this matter, it means that the government is not to be blamed for trying to settle the problems of federal-provincial relations on a unilateral basis, that is to say on its own terms. There can be no question of settling the problem of federal-provincial relations without consulting the other provinces. We have heard all kinds of statements, all kinds of promises in this regard. We were promised a conference. There has been a sham federal-provincial conference, where the government listened and then said that the conference should be guided by a spirit of cooperation. Le Devoir for September 18, 1957 reported as follows:
The Prime Minister had then stated that the next conference might be final or might simply clear the way for another conference where more work would be done.
"The provinces will have their say on the matters to be discussed and on the date of the discussions", the Prime Minister added. "We shall be guided by a spirit of co-operation. The provinces will have the privilege of making recommendations on the most desirable action."
The Prime Minister's office has added that this latter statement was contained in the invitations subsequently sent to the premiers of the ten provinces.
30, 1959
Dominion-Provincial Relations
The press release simply states that the next conference will be called "to discuss a review of tax sharing arrangements".
The Prime Minister listened. The Minister of Finance listened. And when everything was over, the Minister of Finance spoke to the representatives of the various provinces and said: "Gentlemen, we understand your problems, but all your demands would require $1J billion from the federal treasury".
There is the kind of co-operation we had been promised in the 1957 and 1958 election campaigns.
A conference had been announced for 1958. Then there were telegrams. If I may refer to a phrase used by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion), this was not a matter of having the knife at one's throat, but I think it was even worse, because in that telegram, the provinces were not even asked for their views.
The speech from the throne referred somewhat tersely to federal provincial relations. There was talk of co-operation. What is the government waiting for to call a federal provincial conference?
I would like to quote the remarks that the hon. Minister of Finance made on April 28, 1954 when he used to sit on this side of the house.
As can be seen on page 4213 of the official record, the hon. member for Eglinton said:
It is imperative that there be called a dominion-provincial conference. Only the Prime Minister of Canada can call a dominion-provincial conference. The agenda for that conference must include this whole field of taxing powers and responsibilities. It must take due account of the necessity of honouring and respecting, both in the letter and in the spirit, all existing agreements. It must seek in the long run, under the proper auspices and with a patriotic Canadian spirit, to secure a better deal than any of the provinces have had as yet. It would mean an end, Mr. Speaker, to a situation such as that which now has arisen and for which this federal government must accept responsibility.
In the same speech, the hon. member for Eglinton stated another reason which, to my mind, has demagogic overtones. As a matter of fact, we further find on that same page of Hansard dated April 28, 1954, that the hon: member had this to say:
Is it not a strange contradiction, is it not an amazing commentary on the attitude of the government opposite, that at this very moment at

Dominion-Provincial Relations Geneva representatives of the Canadian government are sitting around a table with representatives of communist governments, Russia and China, to discuss matters of at least common concern, yet the Canadian government will not bring itself to sit down with fellow Canadians representative of the provinces to discuss matters of common concern?
I think the hon. member might have given sufficiently good reasons at that time to ask that a federal-provincial conference be called, without having to resort to concepts that might rouse all sorts of feelings and thoughts amongst Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, one of the favourite defenses that this government and its ministers resort to when we accuse them of failing to do their duty or to keep their promises, is to tell us, after picking up a sheet of paper and asking their secretaries to do some careful research work: "In such and such a year, you did exactly the same thing in another field."
Mr. Chairman, when is this government going to stop behaving this way? It is behaving like a 15 year old boy who, on being called down by his father for staying out till 11 o'clock or midnight the night before, answers: "My big brother who is 30 didn't get in till four this morning".
This government has no business recalling what we did when we were in power. On two occasions, the Canadian people rendered its judgment. There is no purpose in recalling the fact and perpetually harping on the former Liberal administration's actions when it was administering the country. However, Mr. Chairman, there will be an appeal against the decision the people have rendered on two occasions since 1957, and when that appeal is heard, the present government, including the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, will be judged according to their own actions and not according to the deeds of the former Liberal administration when it was at the helm in Ottawa.
Mr. Chairman, present developments in the field of federal-provincial relations repeat themselves in many other fields and departments of the federal government.
Everybody remembers the decision which affected more than 14,000 workers in Toronto last February and, at this point, I want to read out a sentence from an item published in the Globe and Mail of February 23, 1959, with regard to this administration's decision and I quote:

(Text):
This weakness has been apparent since the government assumed office 20 months ago: but never, in that time, has it been so dramatically disclosed.
(Translation) :
Mr. Chairman, what is happening at the present time is not limited to the field of fiscal relations; it also applies in several other fields. We could even apply to the present government much more aptly and truthfully today what the present Minister of Finance said of the Liberal government in 1957 when he was sitting in the opposition. In fact, as recorded on page 2559 of Hansard of March 21, 1957, speaking of the Liberal government, the hon. member for Eglinton said:
-a government floundering in the welter of its own incompetence, errors, contradictions and arrogance! These are the fruits of this government; and in the words of Holy Writ, ye shall know them by their fruits.
Mr. Chairman, government members often accuse us of merely criticizing. I should therefore like to close my brief remarks with a suggestion to the government. The field of federal-provincial relations is a very complex one; it must require the federal government's daily attention. I do not believe we can solve those complex questions in a two-day conference held each year or every three years, unless we manage to develop some organization or even a department whose sole duties would consist in studying those matters and keeping in touch with the ten provinces of Canada. That is a question of vital importance to the federal government and the ten provinces, as well as to the municipalities and school boards.
It seems to me the government should consider that suggestion. Besides, I do not claim credit for the idea, for I have heard it expressed by other colleagues on many occasions. However, I am of the opinion that if the government seriously wished to consider the opportunity of setting up a department of federal-provincial relations, there would be no need for calling a conference every two or five years to tell the provincial representatives: "We understand your problems, but we can't do any more than this".
If the government set up a department of federal-provincial relations, it would gain much more co-operation, not only in the field of taxation but also with regard to public works and education, as well as in sectors of common concern to the federal and provincial governments.
I sincerely thank the Minister of Finance for listening to my humble remarks and I hope he will take them into consideration.

Mr. Chairman, our friends in
the official opposition have chosen the occasion of the debate on this resolution to bring up the whole problem of fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces. If the discussion had remained within the terms of the resolution, a debate of such scope would not normally have been allowed. I shall only make a few remarks which are prompted by the speeches made this afternoon in the house by the hon. members for Hull (Mr. Caron) and for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard).
Mr. Chairman, I must say at the outset that I am rather surprised at the statements made by the hon. members for Hull and Lapointe, because they prove the former government's fiscal formula to have been a failure.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall deal
with that question in a moment.
I claim that the remarks of those hon. members show that the system has proved a failure, because at the present time no province is satisfied with it. The fact is that this very complex problem cannot be solved through a simple conference, as the hon. member for Lapointe agreed a moment ago.
When the central government convened the provincial representatives in 1957, it listened to their proposals, but soon realized that there were such differences of opinion between them that it became necessary to go very deeply into that problem.
In other words, the present system has shown that fiscal centralization can never really work in Canada, a country with a federative regime. The important thing would be to find a formula which would hand back the provinces their responsibilities in fiscal matters. That responsibility is essential so that provinces can fully exercise their rights in the field of legislation. Those responsible for the present situation, though they do not like to be told, are the Liberals. They are the ones who during the war, took over the main sources of revenue and who, after the war was over, refused to restore them to the provinces. They are the ones too who, having got hold of those considerable revenues, surreptitiously invaded many other exclusive provincial fields.
Today those people are watching our attempts to solve the problem, and realizing how they messed up the whole thing, how they complicated the fiscal system in this country, they keep telling us: just try to untangle the skein.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
The problem of fiscal relations between Ottawa and the provinces reminds me of an iceberg, only a tenth of which shows above the surface. Actually, Mr. Chairman, the government must be put in a position where, through this legislation, it can keep on arranging meetings and other preliminary talks between the Minister of Finance and the provincial ministers to a new federal-provincial conference, in order to find a lasting formula and not only expedients. It is to be hoped, Mr. Chairman, that once that durable formula is found, it will recognize two principles. First of all, the maximum fiscal responsibility of the provinces. If all provinces were equally empowered to levy revenue, there would be no serious problem involved in allowing them to raise the funds needed to meet their obligations under the constitution. It would only be a matter of distributing the various taxes between the federal government and the provinces. The difficulty today is that several provinces are unable to raise the funds they need, and therefore have to be helped financially. Of course the present system was an attempt to settle this problem, but it considers such assistance as a basic rule rather than an exceptional and temporary one. However, subsidies to the provinces should not be considered as a permanent feature. First, a way should be sought to enable the legislatures to raise their own funds, before asking Ottawa to grant them money that is collected across Canada by the central government, and for which the legislatures are not responsible to the people.
The second principle is that we must recognize the necessity of helping the economically weaker provinces. But this, again, must be a temporary rule. I am confident, Mr. Chairman, that eventually the solution found by this government will rest on those two principles, and then we shall be back to the true spirit of Confederation.
The system devised by the Liberals over 14 years ago has created a bad habit. It is known that several provinces, rather than increase their own tax rates, come here and ask the federal government for subsidies to supplement their budget. This practice is the result of the system adopted by the Liberals, and it is really the basic obstacle to a settlement of the problem. That is why I think we must proceed slowly, and as suggested in this resolution, extend the present system for a period of one year while granting the provinces a further three per cent. But the very fact the government is seeking permission to extend the system for a single year is an indication that it does not intend to maintain a system which, again, has proved inadequate and which truly

Dominion-Provincial Relations shackles the fiscal responsibility ol the provinces, and which must necessarily be discarded. I truly believe that the spirit of confederation requires that the provinces be sovereign and be able to use their taxation powers. Again, the present system does not allow this.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say a brief word or two on this admittedly complex subject of dominion-provincial fiscal relations. I want to comment on only one phase of the resolution. The resolution provides us with the opportunity to bring to the attention of the house and the country another broken promise of the government. All Canadians remember the Conservative election and pre-election promises to call at once a dominion-provincial conference to improve the existing agreements with the provinces and to settle this matter on a long term basis. Hansard is filled with the utterances of hon. members opposite on this subject when they sat on this side of the house and newspaper files across the country are loaded with statements on the matter. But I can do better than that. I can read from an interesting document I have here. This is a statement of policy of the Conservative party and that aspect of its dealing with federal-provincial fiscal relations, as found in paragraph (d), reads as follows:

We will provide for the development in conference with the provinces of a long-term solution of dominion-provincial fiscal relations.
Two elections and almost two years later what has happened? This promised Utopia in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements has not been delivered. In fact, with the passing of the second election the ministry is suddenly strangely silent on this very important subject.
Most Canadians are familiar with the series of incidents over these last two years. At a politically appropriate time the provincial premiers were called to Ottawa with appropriate publicity. Pleasantries were exchanged, some speeches were made, several pictures were taken and more promises were made to meet again soon. There the story seemed to end.
It is true that a small election bone was thrown to the provinces in the unusual form of telegrams, again with appropriate publicity, just conveniently prior to the March 31, 1958 election. However, these election bones shrunk from the time they were promised, which was before the election, to the time they were delivered, which, of course, was after the election. I am thinking now of the Ontario story. The promise there was something of the order of $22 million

or $23 million and I understand that when delivery was made the amount was substantially less due in part, of course, to the economic slow-down for which the government must assume a fair share of the responsibility.
This Ontario story is indeed an interesting one. It was a romance born of political expediency and frustrated ambition. Canadians living in Ontario particularly remember clearly the political shenanigans between Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. Frost. They co-operated to lead the voters in Ontario down the primrose path. Most people remember those happy, reckless days of love and mutual appreciation for each other. Today, the two principal stars of the show, each for his own reasons, would like the public to forget their earlier alliance and avowed aims to correct the wrongs in the field of federal-provincial relations.
Perhaps I should, for the benefit of those who might need their memories refreshed, refer briefly to a couple of items on this subject. There is one appearing in the Globe and Mail, which is scarcely a Liberal organ, under the heading, "Frost Views PM as new FDR". This article goes on to say:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker. Premier Frost and the Conservative members of the Ontario legislature had a love feast over lobster and other cold delicacies yesterday at Queen's park.
By the time they reached the coffee and the end of two short, so-called non-political talks, the two leaders had cemented the mutual security pact born of last year's campaign and, equally important, last June's victory..
What they were doing for each other, they said, they were really only doing for Ontario and Canada.
The luncheon was a re-run of one held last February and MPP's who attended both said they detected an ever greater air of cordiality.
Along the same vein, to substantiate this alliance and to enter into the spirit of it, I would quote what the Prime Minister said about the premier of Ontario. This is taken from the Montreal Star of February 18, 1958. He said:
"Your co-operation, your counsel, your advice and, above all, your wisdom, has meant more to me than I can ever possibly pay an adequate tribute to."
It was a case of love in a cold climate as snow swirled in the stingingly-cold wind outside.
Then, the article continues:
But the political climate couldn't have been warmer.
We all remember Premier Frost's demands for an extra $100 million. I do not need to detain the house on that particular point. We all remember Premier Frost's appearances. We can all think of one in particular in which he turned to the present Prime Minister and said, "There sits the man who will give Ontario its just dues; there sits the man from

whom we will get this $100 million." There were statements of this kind. In order to avoid any misunderstanding about that, I should like to quote briefly from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail after the election. This refers to the $100 million, which was still Ontario's aim. It reads:
Premier Frost still expects to get the balance of the $100 million he suggested to Ottawa last year would be a fair division of tax revenue.
He forecast yesterday that the dominion-provincial conference which adjourned last November will be resumed before July 1 and that Ontario's just needs would be satisfied.
What has happened since March 31, 1958?
I suggest that if Premier Frost had wanted a conference one could aasily have been held. If the Prime Minister had wanted a conference one could easily have been held, as promised.
Now, what can one conclude from all this? Is Mr. Frost waiting to slide through another election, hoping the voters will not remember this hoax? Is the Prime Minister waiting for important provincial elections to be held before disposing of this matter? Who knows? Is there to be a new approach or will we simply be called upon, as we are in this resolution, to extend this arrangement a year at a time? After almost two years in office the Conservative government has failed to do what they said they would do if given the opportunity to form a government.
There is another aspect of this matter upon which I should like to speak briefly. Before the elections the Conservatives said they would leave more room in the direct taxation field for the provinces. Let us look at what has happened. In the field of corporation taxes we find that before the Conservatives took office this tax rate was 47 per cent. The provinces were returned 9 per cent or practically one-fifth, and the federal government retained 38 per cent. Today, after the election, as a result of the recent Conservative budget, the provinces will receive proportionately less in the field of direct taxes. With the election safely behind them, they have moved in the opposite direction. The provinces will still receive only 9 per cent, in spite of the increase in the rate of tax on corporate income to 50 per cent, and the federal government will retain 41 per cent. This is just another example of broken Conservative promises.
The Minister of Finance, by increasing the federal government's slice in this particular field of direct taxation in his budget, has given us a peek at new government policy. You will remember the minister advised us in his budget speech that the federal government would be borrowing less in 1959-60 than last year. He indicated that this would leave 66968-9-203

Apparently a new Conservative government policy on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements has emerged. What they are saying, in effect, is: We will tax more, and you borrow more. This is a further example of broken promises.

speechtext:
I will refer to that in a few minutes.
When this resolution was introduced the Minister of Finance said that the purpose of the resolution was clear and simple. I certainly believe the purpose of the resolution is clear, but I do not believe it is that simple. I am sure that this resolution is one that is of deep concern to the provinces across this country. They have to bring down their budgets and arrange for their year's work. There is some of this work that will take more than one year, and yet they are dependent on the federal government for payments to be made to them based on an annual resolution in parliament. They have no assurance that these payments are going to be made. After all, this government is not one that is noted for observing its election promises or even its contractual obligations, for that matter. The provinces have no guarantee, therefore, that these payments are going to continue.
I believe the time has arrived when this government should meet with the provinces and decide on some arrangement that will at least give the provinces a fairly long term outlook and enable them to arrange their own affairs. There is no need to go into the long list of election promises. We all know what they were. In fact, the government has now become so embarrassed by the continued repetition of those promises that they have decided to divide them into two classes; those that are not so sacred

Dominion-Provincial Relations and those that are sacred; those that are made outside the House of Commons and those that are made inside. It is a little bit difficult to see what use the members of the cabinet will be able to make of such an argument, but I think it is understandable.
Then there were the promises before the election of 1957 and before the election of 1958. We all know what happened. There was the so-called conference, called in November, 1957, and then we had the famous, or infamous, telegrams of the Minister of Finance, and then later the take it or leave it attitude of the government by declaring an increase of 3 per cent on the income tax arrangements. At the conference held in November I remember the Prime Minister said that this would be no take it or leave it attitude; but when a similar resolution came before this house on January 25 last year the provinces were told it was going to be increased from 10 to 13 per cent for one year. There was no agreement; it was just a unilateral action and could not be described as anything but a take it or leave it attitude.
On February 9 exactly the same resolution was introduced by the Minister of Finance. Again there was no agreement between the central government and the provinces; it was a decision made by the central government, and as far as the provinces were concerned they could take it or leave it. I believe we live in a country where it is absolutely imperative that there should be sharing of responsibilities between the central government and the governments of the different provinces. There is no sharing of responsibility in a resolution of this type. As I said before this is nothing more than a unilateral action and the provinces have to like it or lump it.
As far as the maritime provinces are concerned I agree that special grants have been made to them, and I would be one of the first to commend the government for the action it has taken in this respect. But let me say this. These grants have been made not by agreement with the provinces of Canada. I think there is a tremendous difference between making grants to provinces unilaterally and making grants to provinces by agreement. I think agreement between the central government and the provinces is necessary and desirable, and just giving handouts to different provinces, no matter how welcome they may be, is not the proper way to do the job.
Last year, I think on January 25, when the Minister of Finance introduced a similar measure he said it was an interim measure, and an interim measure only. Those words are to be found on page 3796 of Hansard for January 25, 1958. Yet here we are a year later still talking about the interim measure. I think it is about time we had some sort

of meeting with the provinces to find out what agreement can be reached in order to solve the very pressing problems which now face different provinces across the country. I believe that the way this thing is being handled by the government is one example of the piecemeal policy they have adopted for nearly two years now. They have no long term guiding policy; if they have there has been no announcement of it, and there has certainly been no sign of it. They are approaching many of the very important problems in this country on a temporary footing, just to solve the problem for now and avoid the responsibility of having to make any long range policy by which the present government can be guided, by which the governments of the different provinces can be guided, and by which the people of this country can be guided.
Mr. Chairman, everybody recognizes that this is not a simple problem. It is indeed a very complicated one, and I think it is for that reason that more effort should be made by the present government to tackle this problem in some sensible way. Certainly there is no permanent arrangement. I do not think there is any permanent arrangement which can be made between the central government and the provinces in this particular problem. I think it is one which can be solved only for a short period of time, and then further meetings must be held in order to arrive at some arrangement which will carry on for a few more years. But I do not think it is possible to find a permanent solution. It seems to me that the method by which the government is handling this question is nothing more than asking parliament every year for an annual reprieve from their election promises and from their responsibility to the people of this country.
We live in a country which has its central government and its different provincial governments. We live in a country which is governed by unity within multiplicity, and until all parts of this country have their fair share of the great things with which this country is endowed there will always be parts of the country which will be particularly well off and other parts which will not be so well off. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I say that this country will only be a good place for some of us to live in when it is a good place for all of us to live in.

Mr. Chairman, before the introduction of the budget, I had not intended to speak on this matter, but when I saw the strange table on page 2410 of Hansard, I decided to look closely into these so-called federal contributions to the provinces. I

shall demonstrate that this table indicates an utter disregard for provincial autonomy.
I hope that Conservative members from the province of Quebec will remain in the house to hear the remarks I intend to make later on in my mother tongue. If they have the patience to listen, I will prove to them that the attitude of the present government toward the provinces is paternalistic and quite different from the one which, during the election campaign, their .party had pledged itself to take.
I will also make a few comments about the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn). (Text):
Now I will continue. In order to save the Minister of Finance from the temptation of raising points of order which are not really points of order, I intend to read part of the resolution to show why I am completely within the ambit of this resolution.
Resolved-
I may say I am not resolved about this; very far from it.
-that it is expedient to introduce a measure-
They are the governing words of the resolution, that it is expedient to introduce a measure. Mr. Chairman, you just cannot have a one-sided debate; at least not in the kind of parliament we have in a free country under British parliamentary institutions. If you are able to argue that it is expedient, you are likewise able to argue it is inexpedient. I propose to argue that as long as the government has the kind of attitude to the provincial governments that it has demonstrated since it came into office it is not expedient year after year, as my hon. friend from Humber-St. George's said so well a moment ago, to give the government an annual reprieve from its promises. That is a phrase which I wish I might have coined myself, and on which I compliment the hon. member. It expresses very neatly what we are being asked to do, and what we will be asked to do again, I predict, as long as the government has-and here I quote the hon. member for Eglinton when he was on this side of the house-"a servile majority". As long as that obtains we will have to do this in 1960 and again in 1961, and then possibly, but only possibly, they may call a conference before the election of 1962 or the expiry of this set of agreements in order to give some more election promises. But more likely the Minister of Finance, whoever he may be, will send out another lot of telegrams telling the provinces that things will be the same as before; or if things go on the way they have 66968-9-203J
Dominion-Provincial Relations been going financially since this government came into office conditions will probably be a good deal worse.
Now I want to examine, as I indicated in my opening remarks, this table which the minister put on record in Hansard on April 9 at page 2410 and which he was pleased to describe as the federal contributions to the provinces in millions of dollars. Let us see what this government, which pretended to be a champion of provincial rights, calls a federal contribution to the provinces. It calls the statutory subsidies a federal contribution to the provinces. But they are nothing of the kind. This is a solemn obligation which was placed upon the treasury of this country as one of the terms of confederation. It is not a contribution at all. A contribution is something which we, in this parliament, have the freedom to give or not to give; it is not something which is a constitutional obligation, though I am not sure that the present government understands the difference, judging by some recent announcements about which I intend to say no more at this time.
Next, we have tax rental and abatement, and I hope the hon. member for Quebec South is listening to this. What are tax abatements? A tax abatement is an amount by which the federal tax is reduced in order to allow a provincial government to collect its own taxes. In other words, what the minister is claiming in this table is that the taxes which the legislature of Quebec imposes and collects are federal contributions. I do not think Mr. Duplessis ever made so extravagant a claim as that. The idea that money which is collected by a province on its own responsibility and put into its own treasury could ever be called a federal contribution is almost too far-fetched to be credible.
Let us turn, now, to tax rental. What is a tax rental? It is a certain sum paid to a province for relinquishing temporarily its right to impose a similar tax. It belongs to the province, and when we were in power we always said that it belonged to the province; it was in no sense the property of this parliament or of the federal government. All that happened was that as a matter of convenience to the taxpayers in the provinces which desired it-and only in the provinces which desired it-taxes could be imposed by this parliament, collected by the minister of national revenue and then paid over to the provinces. But it was always the property of the province, and we never said anything different. And now we have this government, which claims to be the champion of the
3202	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations provinces, calling that a contribution to the provinces. Of course, it is nothing of the kind.
Next, we have this 50 per cent share of income tax on power utilities. Here again we have a tax which, it is true, is collected by the federal government. It is collected only on those utilities which are privately owned, because the publicly owned utilities are not taxed, and it was felt that it was unfair that the federal authority should receive the full tax on the privately owned ones when it did not tax the publicly owned ones. For this reason it was agreed to split this revenue between the two governments. This money had never belonged to us and we, while in office, never said it did, for the reason that the provinces, had they so wished, could have collected it directly themselves. Here is another example of what might be called the Diefenbaker largesse, and again this largesse is just as phoney as most of the other promises made by hon. gentlemen opposite.
And then we have the term 29 award to Newfoundland which the minister said had been paid, although later he had to admit he was only going to pay when parliament so decided and I hope that it will not be long before this has been done.
If we look again at this list we find two more items, equalization and stabilization, to which I will refer in more detail later, but first I wish first to deal briefly with these so-called conditional payments. I do not intend to go into detail with regard to them because I do not wish to take too long. What are these conditional payments? They represent sums appropriated by this parliament, mostly under Liberal initiatives, for very good causes such as agriculture, health, hospital insurance, welfare, vocational training, highways, resources development and slum clearance, and when we appropriated money for slum clearance we did not use it as an excuse to interfere in provincial administration.
These are fields in which, in our wisdom, we in this parliament, or in previous parliaments, decided it would be advantageous to spend money collected from the taxpayers of Canada. And we said we would spend it if the provinces would match the money. This is not a contribution made by the government to the provincial treasuries at all. It does not help the provinces with their normal financing in any way whatever. Indeed, as the late Angus Macdonald and as Mr. Douglas Campbell, the former premier of Manitoba, frequently pointed out, they often forced a province to go ahead
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

with things at a time when there might be some doubt about their ability to pay for them at the time.
The main point is that this is not a contribution to the provinces. These payments are a very good thing, of course, in every one of the cases I have mentioned, and I say so because they were all brought in by Liberal governments. But they were things done for the benefit of the Canadian people; they were not done for the provinces, and to call these payments contributions to the provinces is just another indication of this centralizing mentality, this attitude that the government is the source of everything, and that it gives everything, whereas, of course, there is no giving involved at all.
Then we have this third category-the most absurd of all-the university grants. Mr. Chairman, university grants do not go to the provinces; they do not go to the provincial treasuries. Indeed, the provincial governments have nothing to do with them, except to the extent that they say which institutions are universities. In no way whatever are university grants related to the provinces. These payments are contributions made for very good and sufficient reasons, and I have no doubt this government also believes that to be the case, because it has increased them by 50 per cent. I am glad the government has done that, although I doubt whether the hon. member for Quebec South would say so, or some of his colleagues who, having got elected on the pledge that they would abolish university grants, came here and voted to increase them by 50 per cent. However, I think they are a good thing, and this is an increase in expenditure which was a great deal more justified than most of the other increases which have brought our expenditures to unprecedented heights-

-such as all the money paid to McKim's and all the additions to travelling expenses. But I do not intend to be diverted from my speech into making the speech of the hon. member for York-Scarborough. Next on this list, in paragraph C, we have "grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal government property". This is described as a contribution to the provinces, and it is so ridiculous that it is not even worth wasting words upon. We have left, in the whole of this table, just three items: equalization payments, stabilization payments and the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Everywhere I have been I have given the government full credit for the Atlantic provinces grants. I think they are a good thing. I wish we had felt that we had been able to make them when we were in office. But I would remind hon. members that between 1956 and 1957 the increases, not in grants or contributions but in the share of the taxation that went to the provinces of this country as a result of Mr. Harris' new deal, were very much higher than the Atlantic provinces grants. In fact, they were three or four times as great, though the Atlantic provinces grants were a good and needful thing and I give the government full credit for them.
The equalization payments and the stabilization payments are, of course, grants to the provinces. That, I admit, and I admit it with the more enthusiasm because this was a Liberal achievement, one of the greatest Liberal achievements of our domestic policy, and, I may say, one which was opposed bitterly by the Tory party from start to finish. Mr. Drew did his utmost when he was premier of Ontario to prevent it. He attacked it unsuccessfully all the time he was Leader of the Opposition. My friend the hon. member for Lapointe this afternoon recalled the attitude that the hon. member for Eglinton expressed in this house as recently as 1956. Indeed, this whole equalization policy was a policy which the Tory party was pledged to end. The Solicitor General said that this basis of grants was a wicked thing and as soon as his government got into office they would change the whole basis but we have not heard much on that subject from the Solicitor General since he became a minister of the crown. Of course, we understand the rules of cabinet solidarity; at least some ministers observe it.
In the year 1957-58 the amount of the equalization payment was $136 million and the amount of the stabilization payment was $3,400,000; that is to say, a total of approximately $140 million. That represented some small increase over the previous year in the equalization feature-a very small increase indeed-but the bulk of that $140 million was the direct result of the formula in the taxsharing law as it was enacted by this parliament in 1956 when the Liberals were in office. There has been only a small increase in these payments to the provinces apart from the Atlantic provinces grants since this government came into office. In fact, the word "contributions" is used rather than "payments" and indeed if they were payments it might have been another matter, but the only contributions since this government came into power apart from the Atlantic provinces grants were the equalization features of the 3 per cent we are talking
about today and the equalization aspect of this is, of course, a relatively small proportion of the total amount which I have not taken the time to work out but which no doubt the minister could give to the committee.
In order to indicate how very different that is from what the minister said the members of his party were going to do, let me remind the committee of one or two things he said as recently as last year. I have here extracts from several speeches and broadcasts he made. Perhaps I should read this to the hon. member for Quebec South. This is an extract from a speech made by the Minister of Finance on the French television network program, "Les Affaires de l'Etat", on November 24, 1958. This was after the election. It was even after the Montmagny by-election. As closely as I can make out it is an exact repetition and an accurate translation of what was said in the Montmagny by-election and that is perhaps why it was repeated. It reads as follows:
(Translation):
In the same way, we have respected provincial rights. We have injected into federal-provincial relations a new spirit of co-operation and respect. And so it is estimated that under the new taxsharing formula with the provinces-
The new formula is exactly the same Liberal formula.
-the new tax-sharing formula with the provinces, Quebec will receive $19 million more than under the Liberal government.
(Text):
Again claiming that the taxes that Quebec collects itself are a contribution from this generous government. I continue: (Translation):
We have increased the provincial share of each tax dollar paid by the Canadians, thus reducing proportionately the federal share.
(Text):
That was before the budget; it is all changed now and in fact it is just the reverse. I continue:
(Translation):
Unlike the Liberals, we are not-
(Text):
That is a real joke. I continue: (Translation):
-we are not centralizers, but constitutionals. (Text):
That was also before the Prime Minister's statement of March 25, this claim that the Conservatives were constitutional. I do not want to sit down without saying a word or two about what was said a while ago by the hon. member for Quebec South. He said that the Liberal scheme was impossible and un-

Dominion-Provincial Relations satisfactory. Why? Why was this Liberal scheme unsatisfactory? What was the great reason? He said:
(Translation):
None of the provinces are satisfied.
(Text):
I think that is evident. It is still true and in 1962 it will still be true and when the hon. member and I are both dead it will still be true. There would be something dead about any federal state in which both national and provincial authorities were fully satisfied with the fiscal relations, because the people who are elected to look after provincial affairs have a responsibility to do the best they can for the people of their province and they are never really going to admit they have enough money to do it, especially when they think they can get the money from the generous Minister of Finance. The hon. gentleman need not think that a new formula is going to change that very much.
What will be disturbing to many people and I am sure it was extremely disturbing to the friends of the hon. member for Quebec South and those of the Minister of Finance in the province of Manitoba was something else he said. He trotted out the old Tory idea which I thought the Prime Minister buried during the 1957 election when he spoke in Manitoba. He did not talk about it in Ontario but when he was in Manitoba he apparently got in a funk and declared, "We believe in equalization, too. We are just as much in favour of equalization as the Liberals are." Here we have the hon. member for Quebec South coming back with the old doctrine under which they would divide up the tax fields and let the provinces collect their own taxes and the federal government collect its own taxes and everybody would be happy. I will tell the hon. member that if the people in Quebec did the arithmetic they would not be very happy about this doctrine but I am not now talking about Quebec, I am talking about Manitoba where more than any place this doctrine of equalization was devised by Mr. Bracken and Mr. Garson many years ago when we had the problems that we had in the thirties in the western provinces.
I can tell the hon. member that any politician, no matter what party he belongs to, who goes out and tells the people in Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland or even Alberta, I suspect, that equalization is going to be done away with and the provinces can raise their own revenues-

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
wants to tell us what he did say, he can correct me as soon as I am finished. What I understood him to say was that temporary aid would be given to the poorer provinces when they needed it but that it should be temporary. The plain fact is that at least six of the provinces in this country all the time, if they have to depend upon the taxes that they can collect within their own borders, will not be able to give decent Canadian services to their people. That is the whole reason for equalization. That is why we did it and that is why we Liberals are proud of it. We believe that if Canadians are going to have an equal citizenship they must have at least a rough approach to equality of services and opportunities.
This notion that in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Newfoundland or even in Quebec you can impose a level of taxation and raise enough money there to provide provincial services without imposing punitive taxation upon the people is just not a fact. Of course, it can be done in Ontario. Why? It can be done in Ontario because of the protective tariffs and many other economic advantages that Ontario now has, not all of which are natural advantages, though many of them are.
What was the system we had at the beginning of confederation? Why do we have those statutory subsidies mentioned in that table? We have them because in 1867 Quebec would not have entered into confederation without statutory subsidies. Nova Scotia got them raised within three years of confederation. New Brunswick would not have come in without the statutory subsidies. The only people who would have been satisfied with this system of having provincial revenue raised exclusively through taxation were the people of Ontario. For a long time they will continue to be the only province where that would work. Unless we want to have disunity, division and inequities in this country, that would not be tolerable at all.
Although I do not think it is expedient to be asking us here in this parliament every year to pass this same resolution and do this same thing, I do say that the fundamental policy, of which this resolution is a small amelioration, a very small amelioration, as I think I have shown in what I have said, is fundamentally and basically a good policy; and the best reason for contending that it is, is the fact that after two years in office the ingenious and hard-working Minister of Finance, with all those commitments behind him and all those promises behind him, has not been able to devise anything better.

This government will not meet the provincial governments in conference. Why? Because they have nothing new to suggest, and they have now called-and I refer to the speech from the throne, and there was no motion about this subject, sir, since you are beginning to get restive-they are going to ask civil servants of the federal government and the provincial governments to try to get together and work out some ideas for them.
Where are those wonderful ideas that the Solicitor General had before the election that were going to sweep this rotten Liberal system out of existence and put something better in its place? Where is this better thing? It is just another vision, sir, and it is worth about as much as the rest of the vision.
