maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel that at this time dominion-provincial relations are at a very low ebb. I think the government is getting a decided bad reaction from the provinces, not only because of what the government is doing but the manner in which it is being done.
The resolution which is before us at this time will carry into effect for another year the motion and the provisions which are being followed at the present time. We had expected that, as a result of many promises made in the recent election campaign, there would have been a new arrangement worked out on a satisfactory basis with the provinces by mutual agreement in a way which would improve provincial financing. Before the
30, 1959	3205
Dominion-Provincial Relations election the government seemed to keep in mind the long complaints that the provinces have had as to the need of additional revenue, and seemed to take the feelings of the provinces into account; but immediately the election was over the government's consideration for the welfare of provincial governments seemed to come to an end.
On January 25, 1958, as reported at page 3795 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance, in announcing the formula that is today being discussed, had this to say:
The estimated cost to federal treasury is over $62 million. This is an interim measure pending reconvening of dominion-provincial conference to seek fiscal settlements.
This was the message that was sent out to the provinces. We are waiting, Canada is waiting, for this solemn commitment to be fulfilled. Instead of the government having brought about an agreement, if possible by mutual discussion, by mutual arrangement, the government at this time has sent an ambassador, a civil servant, out to interview officials of provincial governments. This is a unique way, to say the least, to carry on federal-provincial relations. I am certain that no provincial government has asked that this method be followed. I am certain that this type of action by the government is not one that will inspire confidence from the provinces.
We have asked in this house on previous occasions what progress has been made as a result of this one-man ambassador's travels across the country. At this time when we are discussing very large sums of money the minister owes it to the house to give us a progress report, to tell us when, if ever, we are going to be able to get away from this ad hoc method of handling federal-provincial relations.
The present formula that is being proposed by this resolution and that will be continued has a number of faults, one of which from the standpoint of have not provinces and those whose revenues are most inadequate to meet their needs is that the amounts are too low. The second very strong criticism is that although the percentage is fixed there has been no raising of the floor under these grants, so that although the Minister of Finance outlined in the house last year the amount of money that he forecast the provinces would receive because of the increased percentage that was being provided, these increases have not materialized.
One of the main considerations in federal-provincial relations and federal-provincial conferences in the past has been to place under provincial revenues floors that would be maintained in times of falling revenues. That has not been done in this case. There-

Dominion-Provincial Relations fore, the budgets of provincial governments become subject to the failure of the federal government to maintain a buoyant income, and when the federal government fails to provide full employment, full production and an increasing gross national product, provincial revenues suffer. If the government would place a 95 per cent floor under this additional amount as compared with the former amount it would provide a greater measure of stability for the finances of provincial governments.
The crying need in Canada today is to provide stability of provincial revenues and to provide the provinces with the kind of revenues they need to maintain the services that are their responsibility. Having regard to the way our federal constitution is drafted, responsibility for most of the main services rests with the provinces. They have the responsibility but the federal government has the ability to raise revenues out of all proportion to the responsibilities of the federal government. Having regard to the services that the provinces must provide, the federal government should act in order to give Canadians in every province the opportunity to enjoy the same level of services that is enjoyed in some provinces.
The action of the government in failing to consult the provinces on a high level basis, its failure to consult the premiers of the provinces, has not been well received. The minister has had certain correspondence with various provincial premiers, and as far as federal-provincial relations are concerned the government's attitude seems to be the same kind of attitude that is prevailing in other quarters. Instead of consultation, instead of mutual arrangements, the federal government says: "You can take it or leave it."
With regard to discussions with the provinces I suggest that the minister himself is guilty of using the kind of language that does not improve federal-provincial relations. Correspondence took place with regard to this particular formula with the premier of Saskatchewan, and the Minister of Finance, replying to a letter written to him by the Hon. T. C. Douglas, premier of Saskatchewan, said in part in a letter dated July 7, 1958:
My dear premier:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of June 23. Notwithstanding your mistaken comments, my letter of June 17 is entirely clear and in accord with the facts. While I doubt if I can usefully add anything to what I previously said, perhaps in view of your apparent misunderstanding of the question some further clarification might have value.
The 1958 amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act is likewise perfectly clear. I therefore find it extremely difficult to believe that one of your knowledge and experience would find it capable of misinterpretation,

particularly in view of the explanation given not only in parliament but through subsequent correspondence.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the language contained in this letter was intemperate, uncalled for and that if it were designed to interfere with normal federal-provincial relations it could not have been drafted in a manner better calculated to achieve that regrettable result. There is much talk of the minister being transferred to another portfolio, that of the Department of External Affairs. I would hope that the new training he is being subjected to would result in an improvement in his attitude so that this kind of language is not used. I do not think that abusive language to a premier of a province is something that should be condoned by parliament or by any member of the House of Commons. It is time that the federal government learned from statements made in the past. Although the statement I am about to refer to was made by the Prime Minister in 1956, it could well have been a comment on federal-provincial relations at this time. This is what he said on July 24, 1956:
I believe this. I think it is fair to say that the attitude taken by the government at the last conference was an arbitrary one. The government simply said, "These are the terms." No opportunity was given for amendment or for amelioration of any terms. The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and the Persians, and how similar that attitude was to the attitude of the government in this house, which is that power makes perfect anything they do.
Instead of taking action on the resolution at this time, the government should be placing before parliament new proposals agreed to by the provinces after full consultation, proposals designed to relieve some of the very heavy burdens now being borne by the provinces, designed to bring about an economy with full employment and full production, designed to strengthen the economic and democratic fabric of the nation.
Federal-provincial relations are at a low ebb. They have been damaged. I hope that the government will reconvene a federal-provincial conference and that it will cease to to delegate to a departmental official a role that in fact should be borne by the Minister of Finance.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Rea in the chair.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
1.	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years each of the graduated rates of tax at present applicable to individuals on taxable income in excess of $3000 be increased by two percentage points and that for the 1959 taxation year each of the graduated rates of tax applicable to individuals on taxable income in excess of $3000 be increased by one percentage point.
2.	That with respect to income of corporations earned on and after January 1, 1959 the 45 per cent rate of tax on taxable income in excess of $25,000 be increased to 47 per cent and the 43 per cent rate of tax on taxable income in excess of $25,000 applicable to corporations deriving more than half their gross revenue from the sale for delivery in Canada of electrical energy, gas or steam be increased to 45 per cent.
3.	That commencing January 1, 1959 the definition of medical expenses exclude those amounts which the taxpayer is not required to pay because they are paid with the assistance of the government of Canada under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
4. That amounts paid on or after January 1. 1959 for iliostomy and colostomy pads, crutches, trusses for hernia and rocking beds for poliomyelitis patients be included in the medical expenses that are deductible in computing taxable income.
5. That for the 1959 and subsequent taxation years an individual be allowed to deduct in computing income, in addition to the amounts now permitted by the act, any amount received by him out of a pension fund or plan upon withdrawal or retirement from employment or upon the winding up of the fund, not exceeding the portion thereof that is paid in the year, or within 60 days after the end of the year, as a contribution to a registered pension fund or plan or as a premium under a registered retirement savings plan.
6.	That with respect to deaths occurring after April 9, 1959 the exemption for a portion of a death benefit paid by an employer upon or after the death of an officer or employee in recognition of his service be changed from an amount equal to the employee's remuneration for the last 90 days in the office or employment to an exemption for an amount equal to the remuneration of the employee for the last 12 months in the office or employment or the amount of $10,000 whichever is the lesser.
7.	That for 1960 and subsequent taxation years there shall be included as income from an office or employment the amount of the benefit which an employee derives by virtue of the payment by his employer of a premium under a group life insurance plan to provide the employee with life insurance coverage to the extent that it is in excess of $25,000.
8.	That the time within which a notice of objection to an assessment issued after February 8, 1959 must be served be increased from 60 to 90 days from the day of mailing of the notice of assessment.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think there is nothing new to be mentioned in connection with this opening paragraph. Mr. Chairman, I do recall the discussion of last year with respect to relevancy and order, and I think I would agree with the minister that providing there is at all times adherence to relevancy it is desirable that an attempt be made for speakers to keep to the individual paragraphs in the resolution in seriatim. My understanding is that in recent years we consider that we have in nine parts a resolution as a whole. The only difficulty I can think of is that some member might come in a bit late and feel that his rights had not been properly respected. I personally would address myself to the resolution in its separate nine parts.
Mr. Chairman, we have, of course, very recently completed a formal debate on the budget. I think that in particular the first two paragraphs of this resolution, Nos. 1 and 2, highlight and pinpoint the general criticism which was advanced to the budget speech of the minister, which I think can be most appropriately advanced to these particular paragraphs. The general phrases, if one were to summarize, which seem most effectively to indicate the feeling of the opposition, and indeed the public as a whole, are that these paragraphs pinpoint the nature of betrayal and the nature of bad faith when one relates the proposals we are now asked to deal with in detail to the promises spree which we heard in two recent elections. In other words, we are today at the point where the promises of yesterday are the deficits and taxes of today.
If there were any key promises of this government that I think most members of 66968-9-204i
Income Tax Act
the public have in mind and which helped bring the government to power, surely they were the seemingly clear pledges that the government would not be increasing taxes but on the contrary would be reducing taxes. In other words, we are asked here in the first two paragraphs to raise the tax rates on individual incomes and on corporation incomes, and I suggest that this is a complete reversal of everything that was advanced to the public by this government. We have a very keen recollection of how my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and those associated with him, not only in the house but on the election platforms, blasted their opponents ever and over again claiming that their predecessors were spending too much and taxing too much. We have in this resolution to amend the Income Tax Act an application of new taxes which involves an increased take from the public by way of income tax of 12J per cent.
I have raised the question before and I raise it again now in the hope that the minister will comment upon it. I would like his comments as to whether or not these proposals may not do the very opposite of what is desired with respect to our economy. I am thinking that these increases in taxes to the extent that they are advocated may actually brake the re-employment that is the desire of everybody, and indeed could very much backfire on the economy of the country at this present stage. I think the minister shares my respect for a certain non-partisan organization that considers tax matters. I refer to the Canadian tax foundation, the director of which is a former very highly respected member of the Department of Finance, Mr. Harvey Perry, even prior to the minister's budget proposals, said and I quote "already taxes are at such a level that they influence, and usually in a detrimental way, almost every aspect of our economy."
The conspicuous thing about the financial proposals which have come from the minister and his government at this present time is that they do not seem to have the recipe which we heard so much about in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958. The Prime Minister has confessed to the trades and labour council and to the municipalities and other delegations since he has assumed office that there was no such recipe which, on the other hand, he indicated he had, namely that you could have a great amount of candy in connection with government administration and not pay for it. I ask the Minister of Finance in his subsequent remarks tonight to indicate his views upon these tax increases in relation to higher prices, more inflation, and the threat to exports; and in particular one thing which is concerning us

Income Tax Act
all at the present time, and that is whether we are, as a result of a built-in tax expense, being taxed out of sales.
I indicated to the minister on budget night that it was a very startling thing to find him budgeting seemingly with mirrors, in that within a very short space of time he had ceased boasting about tax reductions of $178 million in 1957 and was, in this 1959 budget, proposing tax increases of double that amount-$2 increase for every $1 decrease. Increases in taxes in a full year, he says will be $352 million. The most startling thing about it all is that none of these proposals seem to jibe in any way with the long held views which the minister has so long and often expressed in this house. We recall that in the past few weeks we have heard some surprising and cynical remarks from occupants of the treasury benches about the subject of promises, and there seemed to be some priority in connection with their promises, depending on whether they were made inside or outside the House of Commons. But both inside and outside the house the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have gone on record with respect to disapproving tax increases. Their fiscal policies are on record, and have been on record for a great number of years.
I raise this question of money left over for capital expenditure because it seems to me that the fillip that we might expect at the present time, and which would give us the greatest opportunity for the re-employment of those who are now unemployed, could very properly come from the private segment of our economy. This seems to be a view which the minister himself shared in recent times. I would remind the hon. gentleman that on March 27, 1956, as reported at page 2648 of Hansard, he said this:
Canada needs capital. We need capital created out of the savings of the people. That is one reason why the government ought to be making resolute efforts to reduce the burden of taxation on the Canadian people.
I think the finance minister should tell this house why his views seemed to have changed in such a short period of time.
During the budget debate we heard spokesmen of the ministry indicate that a certain amount of economic surgery and unpleasantness was necessary in present circumstances. The Minister of National Revenue suggested that men and women did not always expect from their government policies which involve flavoursome potions and painless surgery. But that is not what this administration said to the Canadian people in the two recent election campaigns. The most charitable thing I can say to the finance minister and to his associates is that perhaps they were so naive and so disrespectful of economic laws that

they actually believed that the advantages which they promised could be achieved without increases in taxation. Either the government must admit that they possessed this naivety-a naivety amounting almost to stupidity-or, on the other hand, they did believe that through high pressure selling they could take the Canadian people as, shall we say, saps, and persuade them to accept the kind of economics they presented to them. But events are catching up with this government and we now see very clearly the cost of the so-called vision.
In the budget debate I did make reference to the new taxes whose imposition the minister was prepared to advocate at the sales tax or consumers' tax level. I find that with respect to the sales tax for old age pensioners, the minister's proposal means that another $93 million would accrue to the treasury from the 1 per cent increase. He expects another $46 million from new imposts on the excise taxes. In other words, a total of $139 million out of $352 million comes from tax on spending. We have already seen how quickly proposals of this kind can be triggered into eventual cost burdens on the consumers in this country, burdens which are far greater than the actual dollar value of the taxes themselves. The Prime Minister exploded over this matter in the House of Commons when replying to a question addressed to him by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Well, these increases might be inexcusable, but the Prime Minister offered no remedy with respect to them. The pages of Hansard over the past ten years are full of statements by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance indicating that this would be the inevitable result of an increase in this particular type of taxation on consumers spending.
I hope that before we conclude our discussion of items one and two, the minister will very carefully explain to this committee why he feels that measures to increase this type of taxation can be advanced by him without the consequences which he himself in the past said were so unfortunate from the point of view of inflation and spiralling costs.

I may say at the outset that the members of this group intend to discuss the items themselves, and not to enter into a general debate on the income tax provisions and similar subjects. I rise on item one to bring to the attention of the minister two or three matters which I have raised in this committee in previous years and which have come to my notice as a result of considerable correspondence from a large number of people who are concerned about the questions I intend to raise.
The first matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention is that while we note

that no general increases in exemptions for income tax purposes have been provided, we in the C.C.F. party do feel that there was an opportunity to assist certain groups of people who are obliged to bear extra expense because of their situation or the conditions under which they live. The first are those working people who live some distance away from their places of employment. This problem becomes ever more acute with the growth of our cities and the necessity which so many people find of moving into suburban areas in order to obtain suitable housing and so on. We feel that some provision should be made for the exemption of at least a portion of the extra expense occasioned by travel in such circumstances.
In the constituency which I have the honour to represent, there are a number of working people who are obliged to travel as far as 30 miles to work each day. This is necessary because they have to live at some distance from their places of employment in order to find satisfactory living conditions for their families. I do urge the minister to give some consideration to allowing at least a portion of this travel expenditure to be exempted for income tax purposes.
The second group from whom I have heard is a group of disability pensioners, and I suggest it would be possible for the minister to assist these pensioners and war veterans without great expense to the treasury while performing a service of particular value to these handicapped persons. I have particular reference to amputees.
I know of several cases where these people are required to hire a taxi to go to their employment because they cannot drive a car or where they are required to use a motor vehicle because they are unable to walk and things of that sort. These men who suffer these disabilities should receive some consideration because of the extra expenses they have to incur in travelling. I bring that to the attention of the minister and would like to have his comments later on in the evening. I have received a number of letters about this matter. The suggestion appealed to me because it seemed to me that the minister could do something for these unfortunate persons who have difficulty meeting the increased cost of living because of disability incurred in the service of their country.
I have also had representations from people with respect to the allowance costs incurred for non-licensed ambulances or methods of transportation used by persons who have to be taken to hospital where it is impossible to employ a licensed ambulance. I know that in a constituency such as I represent, and there must be many others in the same position, if a man is
Income Tax Act
injured in the woods it is sometimes necessary to hire a launch to take him a distance of 20 or 30 miles and then hire a car to take him a distance which in some cases is up to 100 miles, or hire some other form of conveyance. I mentioned last year a case where we had to put an injured man on horseback and take him over the hills for some considerable distance. These are expensive forms of travel. Of course, no one considers expense when taking an injured person to hospital when he is stricken in the woods, the hills or the mines. I have met many people who believe that some consideration should be given by the minister to those much higher costs incurred for performing what is in effect an ambulance service compared with those that have to be paid by persons who can obtain licensed ambulances because they are close to cities where distances are shorter and so on. I urge the minister to give further consideration to this and I should like to hear his comments about those suggestions.
I have received many letters criticizing the limitation of $100 for charitable donations. The argument used in those cases is that it does not properly recognize persons with charitable instincts whether they are donating to churches, hospitals or other charitable causes. There should be provision for a larger exemption in this respect or provision for the amount a person donates to these good causes. That is all I have to say at this point and I shall look forward to hearing the minister's comments later.

Mr. Chairman, the first of these resolutions we have before us tonight is the first concrete indication we have had that the bills are coming in. They are to be met in part through income tax increases and other taxes. These will serve to meet them only in part because some of them will be merely absorbed in the deficit for next year which is still something over $400 million.
When the Prime Minister was speaking on "The Nation's Business" over television on April 20 last, he had something to say about these increases in income and other taxes. I shall quote what the Prime Minister said from the circulated text of his broadcast:
We have put into effect many of the human betterment measures which people have asked for. These have already cost large sums of money and will continue at a high level in the current year.
I agree that they have cost large sums of money and that they certainly will continue at a high level, but some of us remember how these costs were to be met out of the waste and extravagance of previous government expenditures amounting to something approaching $500 million in the

Income Tax Act
estimation of various Conservatives. They said then that these costs for what the Prime Minister calls human betterment measures would be met out of the waste and extravagance of the Liberal administration. In his broadcast the Prime Minister went on to say:
The tax increases in this year's budget-
The increase in the first resolution is an important part of them. I continue:
The tax increases in this year's budget are directly related to the human betterment expenditures. In total, however, the tax increases are much less than the additional payments to alleviate the effects of the recession. The budget is up by $245 million in taxes in the current fiscal year.
I think the minister will support this statement. The increase in taxation for a full year will come to well over $245 million; according to our calculations it will perhaps be $340 million or $350 million. However, leaving that difference aside for the moment, the Prime Minister went on to say:
Even so, the income rates will be lower than when our government assumed office.
Perhaps the minister will confirm that in his remarks. The Prime Minister continued:
On the other hand we will be paying out this year $550 million more to Canadians in national health insurance, welfare and social security payments than in 1956-57, the last year before we came into office. That is to say, twice as much as the tax increases.
"Twice as much as the tax increases," says the Prime Minister using a figure of $550 million and including in that sum payments for national health insurance which employees and employers contribute to and only part of which comes from the government. It is therefore quite a misleading calculation to say the least. Then the Prime Minister went on to say:
The $550 million does not include additional expenditures which will be made for unemployment insurance as a result of the extension of these benefits to more people and for longer periods. Here alone, the additional costs will be $200 million more than in 1956-57. This will bring the total of human betterment measure payments to more than three times the amount of the tax increases.
I would like to see if the minister confirms that the increase in human betterment payments this year will be over $1 billion because the increase in taxes for a full year will be $350 million.
This was the statement made a few weeks ago to the public. The Prime Minister concluded this part of his statement with the following words:
These heavy demands for social and individual security measures to meet the recession effects have resulted in a projected deficit for the current year.
Mr, Chairman, I call your attention to the reason given by the Prime Minister for these heavy demands for social and individual

security measures. He said, as he said previously, they are to meet the recession. That is the purpose, according to the Prime Minister, of these additional social security demands, to meet the recession effects. Are we to draw from that that when these recession effects are over-and the minister says we are on the way out of the recession-these heavy demands for social and individual security measures which have been made to meet the recession are to be withdrawn and this social security program about which the Prime Minister boasted in the early part of his statement is to be reconsidered again?
Perhaps when the time comes the minister will deal with these two matters; the statement made over the air that there have been additional payments for human betterment this year of over $1 billion and the statement made that these heavy demands for social security and other increased payments in this form were made to meet recession effects. Perhaps he will tell us what is to be done about them when the recession disappears as we all hope it will?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that in my part of the country the land is of no use until the brush is removed but there is no provision under which the costs of the removal of brush from the land are deductible from income tax. I would urge the minister to give this matter serious consideration and shall look forward to hearing his comments on this subject.

I gather that the minister will possibly make comment on some of the things that have been mentioned; therefore I would like to leave this thought with him. I hope he may be able to reply to it, since he is thoroughly familiar with the question that I am about to mention, it having been brought to his attention in a formal way on other occasions. I make reference to the question which my friend from Kootenay West raised, notably travelling expenses of industrial workers. The expenses incurred by such people may vary from one part of the country to another and certainly may vary according to the work that a person does; but I should like to relate the problems that the workers on the west coast of British Columbia are confronted with, because of the extraordinarily high travelling expenses they have to meet.
The logging industry on the coast of British Columbia is classified or considered as being a seasonal one. There is during the winter months of December, January

and February, depending on the severity of the winter, a shut-down of the logging industry. Then, in the summer months, depending again on the weather, how dry it is and how low the humidity is, there is a possibility of a shut-down. The summer closures or shut-downs take place at the insistence of the provincial government. Where there is excessively low humidity they may institute forest closure which means that all of the logging camps in the area affected must close down. A logger finding himself confronted with these two problems has in effect at the start of the winter to pay his fare from Vancouver, where most of the hiring is done and then out to the logging camp initially to get started in the spring. If the forest closure comes along, which happened in 1951 in particular and again last year, sometime probably in June, the logger finds that he has to pay his fare back again to Vancouver and then from Vancouver out to the camp again when the forest closure is lifted, and back to Vancouver again when the winter season sets in, say, in the month of January. Therefore, he finds he has to make four single trips or two round trips from the camp at which he is to Vancouver where, as I said, most of the hiring is done. This is an excessively high penalty that he has to pay to become employed and keep employed.
Certainly, I think some consideration should be given in so far as being able to deduct the travelling expenses that a logger, and other industrial workers like him have to incur in order to get out to the job where they are working and back to town again, especially when their travelling is no fault of their own, when it is occasioned by weather, by governmental action in closing the forests or by curtailment of production, as happens from time to time and the camp closes down. Especially in these cases he should have the right to make certain deductions on his income tax return for the money that he spends in getting out to work and providing income for himself and his family.
Also the loggers-again I mention them only because I am personally familiar with their difficulties but this applies to construction workers as well; it applies to miners and it applies to other types of industrial workers- find themselves in this position. Most of the logging camps

I would say 90 per cent of them-have no accommodation for families, or very little. Those that do have accommodation for families are concentrated in the lower portion of Vancouver island where there are quite a number of roads and access transportation is more readily available than it is in the upcoast camps. Practically all

Income Tax Act
of the upper coast camps do not have accommodation for a man and his family. Consequently, practically all of the loggers have to maintain their wives and children, say, in Vancouver or in the Fraser valley, in Westminster. I know many in Burnaby.
Loggers who live there who have to go up to the upcoast camps in order to work find also that they have to pay board and lodging charges to the company for whom they work. They are in effect maintaining two homes, again through no fault of their own. Many of them that I know personally would like to move their families with them where they are working but the policy of the company, the places where the camp is located, the lack of transportation facilities, road, rail or ship, and so on, make it impossible for the person to locate himself and his family at the particular logging camp. Some provision should be made whereby in these circumstances he is able to make a deduction for income tax purposes of the extra money he has to pay out, first to provide board and lodging for himself in the logging camp and second to maintain a home where his wife and family live, which is some place else.
Third, and probably I would consider this the least important of the three, the necessary deductions which I think should be allowed relate to clothing for industrial workers. The argument, of course, which says that this is probably not so important as the other two is that we all have to buy special clothing of some kind. For instance, probably the Minister of Finance has a larger number of blue ties than do loggers in the logging camps or the miners under ground. I imagine we can assume that part of the outlay of the Minister of Finance for clothing should be a deductible expense, depending on the number of blue suits and ties he has. But there are some types of workers who, because of the type of work they are in, have to expend money for particular types of protective clothing which are not required elsewhere. For instances, miners underground need hard hats. They need rubber clothing or sweater clothing to keep dry and they are required also by law to have safety-toed or steel-toed boots.
The loggers out in the bush are in the same position. The compensation regulations require them to wear a certain type of boot to log with on the coast. The logger has to have a cork boot. They have to wear hard hats. They also need other extra types of clothing, depending on the weather. Other types of workmen need special types of gloves, depending on the industry in which they are working. Consideration should be given to these factors also, especially when we look at the cost of some of these protective

Income Tax Act
pieces of clothing which are required by law. A pair of logger's cork boots, for instance, which might last, if he is lucky and does not have to wear them in country that has too much rock in it or is too rough, a logging season, costs somewhere in the neighbourhood of $33 to $35 a pair. If, as we gather from newspaper articles, there is a trend by boot manufacturers to increase their prices, the price of cork boots will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $40 a pair. Many people have to get specially made cork shoes because of the impairment they may have in their feet, and so on. The cost of a pair of such shoes may range as high as $50 or $60 and they last probably only for one season.
I think special consideration should be given to those three items. While I have mentioned loggers particularly, I only do so because of familiarity with them and I am not in any way intending to leave the impression that other industrial workers are in a less favourable position. Certainly they have somewhat the same costs for somewhat the same reasons.
This matter has been brought to the attention of the present minister and to the attention of his predecessor. I know that other hon. members are familiar with the problem and have discussed it with other people. It is obvious that no provision is to be made in these amendments but I would certainly appreciate an indication from the minister as to what action he contemplates in this regard and I hope that the action will be more than the usual statement that the matter is under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, while we are discussing this resolution I should like to point out that great emphasis has been placed in the last number of years on the field of higher education. In that regard I should like to suggest that because the summer work period for students is short some consideration should be given to exempting them from income tax on their earnings in order to encourage them to work. In other words, we should eliminate any retarding factor with regard to their going to work during the summer holidays. I have discussed this problem with quite a number of hon. members and people attending universities and they feel that some consideration should be given to this particular factor as far as income tax is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the idea just put forward by the hon. member for Moose Mountain. I know that all hon. members are interested in the subject of higher education. It is not too long ago, in fact earlier this year, that a brief was presented to the government by the Canadian association of medical students and

internes in association with the national federation of Canadian university students. As a preamble to the brief the following statement by Dr. J. Cyril James, principal and vice-chancellor of McGill University, is quoted:
A young Canadian from a family of modest circumstances has less chance of getting a university education today than a youth in any other country with which I am familiar. It underlines the fact that Canadians have fewer opportunities to obtain a university education.
That is a very serious observation, one which I think we have a responsibility to do something about. The brief goes on to give some statistics. It points out that only 7.2 per cent of students of university age in Canada go on to attend university despite the fact that more than 30 per cent of any given age group being deemed suitable university material. The brief sets out that of those who leave school before completing their education fully 50 per cent do so for financial reasons. The brief elaborates on the difficulties students have in earning sufficient money during the summer to pay their expenses and says that about 80 per cent have to have support from their parents or their spouse. They go on to suggest that without any contravention of the British North America Act the Minister of Finance could assist students in obtaining a university education by making certain amendments to the Income Tax Act and providing for certain deductions from taxable income. The five suggestions they make in their brief are:
1.	The cost of tuition for the student in full time attendance at a Canadian college or university should be deductible from the taxable income of the student or from the taxable income of the person paying this expense, whether that person be parent, guardian or spouse.
2.	The cost of books and instruments for the student in full time attendance at a Canadian college or university should be deductible from the taxable income of the student or from the taxable income of the person paying this expense, whether that person be parent, guardian or spouse.
3.	The present amount which a student in full time attendance at a Canadian college or university may earn and still be claimed as an exemption on the income tax return of parent or guardian should be increased from $950 to $1,100.
4.	The exemption which the parent or guardian of a student in full time attendance at a Canadian college or university may claim, as exemption for the student, should be increased, when this exemption is applicable, to $1,000 from the present $500.
5.	The spouse of a student in full time attendance at a Canadian college or university should be allowed an exemption of $1000 for the student provided that the student not earn more than $1,100 in which case the exemption would be reduced by the amount earned over $1,100 subtracted from $1,000.
The brief and its recommendations were very carefully thought out by a group of interested students who will themselves reap

no benefit but who have at heart the interests of those who will succeed them in academic life. I urge the Minister of Finance to consider these recommendations and to see if he cannot at least accept them partially. I also urge the support of all members of the house, particularly all Progressive Conservative members, for the suggestions put forward in this brief.
On the subject of the changes in taxation, Mr. Chairman, we know that the Progressive Conservative party has always claimed to be consistent in its viewpoint. Therefore I think we might examine the record for a moment to see the nature of their consistency. I have here a document entitled, "What the Progressive Conservative party Stands For." It is a resume of the resolutions adopted by that party at their national convention in December, 1956. Under the heading "Taxation and Trade" the first resolution passed reads as follows:
The Progressive Conservative party will reduce taxation to a level that will result in a balanced budget and eliminate huge surpluses-
They have certainly eliminated the huge surplus already.
-of revenue over expenditure to the end that the individual taxpayer will be given relief from the crushing burden he has been carrying and our producers will be enabled to meet competition better in foreign markets through lower prices for their products.
I think the resolution was excellent, and I am sure the Minister of Finance would be well advised to try to live up to it more closely than he has been able to.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.
Can the hon. gentleman tell me whether the document he is reading from is not a secret document?
I think it has been withdrawn from publication under orders from the present leader of the Progressive Conservative party.
Let's have a duet.
Why don't you sing us a song?

Thank you for the applause. During the election campaign of 1957 the Prime Minister had some other things to say about taxation. The following is part of a report of an address he made in Toronto:
"It is time", he said, "to take the unrepentant taxmasters off the backs of the Canadian people.
. . . The government seems to think it is good for the souls of the Canadian people to overtax them and to have honest Canadians pushed around and pilloried by income tax snoopers. The views of the ivory tower boys seem to be that if you
Income Tax Act
spend your money it makes inflation but if the government takes it from you and spends it, no harm is done."
He went on to say:
When the Conservative party forms the government of this country a session of parliament will be called to reduce taxation.
They were.

Someone said that there was. What is necessary is a postcript to the effect that another session of parliament would be called to put them back up again.
Then, at Quebec on April 27, 1957, the Prime Minister made a statement. The newspaper article reads:
The Liberal government was concentrating taxing power in Ottawa and if that trend continued it would dilute provincial rights as effectively as if the constitution were amended.
Mr. Diefenbaker called the Liberal party "the high tax party" and reiterated his promise that a Conservative government, if elected June 10, will call an immediate session of parliament "to reduce such taxation as can be reduced".
"Don't you think you have been overtaxed long enough by this government?" he asked.
They must have.

I take it, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian people may feel that they have been overtaxed by the present government, and if the Minister of Finance does not show greater consistency between those views put forth by himself and his leader in the days when they were on this side of the house and those which they are putting forward at the present time on the other side of the house, he can expect the Canadian people to pass the same verdict on his administration that he requested them to pass when we were over there.

I think there are a few further observations that ought to be made in connection with the increases in taxes which are now proposed by the Minister of Finance. These increases ought to be related to the situation, as the hon. member for Trinity has just pointed out, described by the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and others concerning the kind of rectification that they would provide if they were given an opportunity of sitting on the ministerial benches.
As the hon. member for Trinity has reminded us, the Conservatives made their appeal to the people in the two last federal elections on the ground that they would provide a reduction in taxation. Undoubtedly that had an important effect on the judgment of the Canadian people. Long before the elections, in session after session, hon. gentlemen opposite complained about the levels of taxation in Canada. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has pointed out

Income Tax Act
that, confronted with the present situation, we should examine the consequences of the administrative policy of the government. The Leader of the Opposition has reminded us of the statement made by the Prime Minister in a recent speech which he made over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation television network on Monday, April 20. I remind the Minister of Finance of certain words in that speech which are to be found on page 3 of the text. The Prime Minister said:
We have put into effect many of the human betterment measures which people have asked for.
Now that, of course, is not an accurate statement. The government did amend certain social welfare legislation, and that is a matter of record. But the fact is that over 90 per cent of the benefits of existing social welfare measures were established by the previous administration under Liberal auspices. It is inaccurate for hon. gentlemen opposite to say that they have put into effect many of the human betterment measures which people have asked for.
Then, the second sentence-
We raised the old age pension.

My hon. friend says that they did raise the old age pension. Yes, the present old age pension is $55 and hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for $9 of that, while Liberal administrations are responsible for $46. It is true that my hon. friends have raised old age pensions, but it must not be forgotten that if the budgetary recommendations that will shortly be considered by this committee are put into effect, then what this government did when it raised old age pensions is now being taken away by additional taxation which they said was not necessary in order to provide the increases in social benefits.
Then, the Prime Minister goes on to say:
In total, however, the tax increases are much less than the additional payments to alleviate the effects of the recession.
Then, he says:
The tax increases in this year's budget are directly related to these human betterment expenditures.
That is not the fact; undoubtedly, some of the tax increases are due to some of the matters relating to programs for human betterment.
Such as hospital insurance.

Introduced by a Liberal administration, and placed on the statute books of this country by a Liberal administration. Hon. gentlemen opposite are now going about the country, not having provided one single social measure, taking credit

for something that was put on the statute books by a Liberal government, and which hon. gentlemen opposed.
Now, the fact is that we are called upon to deal with a proposal for increased expenditures and increased taxes in consequence, expenditures which, session after session, hon. members opposite criticized and said were unnecessary. I regret to say it, but perhaps there was no greater critic of many of these expenditures than the Minister of Finance, who dealt with item after item in the various departmental estimates and complained about the cost of this or that particular item. Yet, what do we find on an analysis of the expenditures proposed in the estimates for 1958-59 as compared with those of 1959-60? I propose to examine a few of these items on a comparative basis to ascertain the extent to which this government, dedicated to the principle of reduction of expenditures and at the same time enthusiastically dedicated to the principle of tax reductions, was able to achieve its stated objective.
The increase in taxes is, first of all, the dominant fact of the moment. In the face of this it will be interesting to examine, as I now propose to do, the extent to which hon. gentlemen opposite, by their administrative policies, have been able to carry out their election promises in regard to these items, as well as the demands which they repeatedly made during the sessions of this parliament over the course of the last decade.
Hon. gentlemen opposite used to complain about the level of professional and special services. The government of Canada was spending too much of the money that parliament was voting on professional services. In the estimates for 1958-59, professional services are 92.9 as compared with the increase in the estimates for 1959-60 to 96.7. In other words, there is an increase in professional services of 3.8 per cent.
Then, when we come to travelling and removal expenses, we find the same thing. Oh, the criticisms that were levelled against every minister who presented his estimates before the period when hon. gentlemen opposite came into office; too much money was being spent on travel by officials, by ministers and by others. Let us examine the situation now. In the 1958-59 estimates the percentage for travel and removal expenditures was 57.7, and in the estimates for 1959-60, they totalled 66.8 an increase of 9.1. This government was going to cut down on travel expenses of all kinds, but the first full year of office the Minister of Finance is estimating for an increase in this particular expenditure of 9.1. Hon. gentlemen are now confronted with a demand for an increase in taxes, and this is one reason, among others,

that there is some necessity for the government to impose additional taxation to meet these additional expenditures which hon. gentlemen opposite said they would reduce.
Then we come to postage. We were told that the government would save all kinds of money if it would encourage a policy of thrift in the amount that was spent on postage in all government departments. In 1958-59, 5.9 was spent on postage, and in the estimates for 1959-60, 6.0, an increase is proposed of close to 1 per cent.
Point one per cent.
That is what I said.
No, you did not.
What did I say?
One per cent.

Then I thank the hon. Minister without Portfolio for discharging his without portfolio ministerial duties.
Then we come to exhibits, advertising, films. We all recall how the Minister of Finance used to fulminate on this subject. Too much money was being spent by all government departments on pamphlets and films. A great saving could be effected and consequently taxes would be reduced if only the government did not spend so much on all kinds of pamphlets, films and so on. Well, in the estimates for 1958-59, the figure is 11.8, and the same figure represents the expenditures in the estimates for 1959-60, but there is no reduction, although the Minister of Finance when a private member of this house said that this was one area where much reduction could be effected.
Well do I remember how on one particular night the then Minister of Finance was joined by his colleague and seat mate, the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood, when he took up pamphlet after pamphlet of the Department of National Health and Welfare. One which I remember was entitled "Recreation Pays Dividends". That caused much mirth at the time. I do not know whether there has been any reduction in the pamphlets of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am not suggesting that there should be. I believe they were all very useful, but what hon. gentlemen forget is that they said that was one very important place where reductions in expenditure could take place.
Then materials and supplies. Too much was being spent by government departments on materials and supplies of all kinds. The situation in 1958-59 was that the expenditure was 179.5, and in the estimates for 1959-60

it was 181.5, an increase of 2 per cent. No reduction there. Too much money was being spent by the government, we were told by the Minister of Finance, in all kinds of unnecessary maintenance work, repairs and upkeep. In the main estimates for 1958-59 the expenditures represent 165.0, and in 1959-60 these repairs and maintenance charges have gone up to 183.5, an increase of 18.5.
One could go on into various other comparisons to indicate the extent to which pledges made by hon. gentlemen, and demands made by hon. gentlemen when in opposition, are not being implemented by them when they now have the opportunity of so doing. Then of course hon. gentlemen complained about the large numbers of people employed in the public service. Too many people were employed to serve the government of Canada; that was the charge of hon. gentlemen opposite. Well, the number of additional men and women serving in the public service is close to 5,000.
It is nearer 9,000.
