speechtext: No.
Close to 5,000 was the last figure I saw, but my hon. friend the Minister of Finance says no. It may be higher than that; perhaps I am underestimating.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend never underestimates.

The minister will find one of his colleagues, in outlining during the course of his speech the efficiency of the public service, referred to an increase of something around 5,000. My hon. friend keeps shaking his head; no doubt he will produce the figures. If he cannot produce the figures contradicting this statement, I can only say to him that if there is an increase in taxes it is because this government has not reduced expenditure as it said it would, and on that account, instead of being able to present the people with a promise fulfilled to reduce expenditures, it is called upon to increase taxation as the result of its failure to observe the principles of thrift and economy which it espoused for so many years when it sat on this side of the house.

Mr. Chairman, after the organ in full symphony I hope you will not mind a toot or two on a whistle! I would like to support very strongly the remarks made by the hon. member for Trinity in relation to some alleviation of or consideration for the problems of people who are going to university, and especially the recognition by the Income Tax Act of the special burdens they

Income Tax Act
have. As I have heard recently about the Conservative party being positive, I thought I would introduce a little of that positive approach into this debate. The only coherent statement I have encountered of the Conservative position today is in the pamphlet "Conservative Concepts", which was published this year and which I hope most of my Conservative friends have read. There appears in this pamphlet a very good article written by an academician, W. L. Morton, called "Canadian Conservatism Now". He stresses a sound philosophy for Conservatism and asks can such a program applicable to present circumstances in Canada be deduced from such an attempt to sketch a Conservative philosophy for our time? He says he believes so, and then lists nine points, and point No. G is the one to which I want to draw the particular attention of the Minister of Finance. It is:
The massive support of the able in education and of research in all fields of knowledge.
At the conclusion of his nine points he says:
You will note that I do not ask that anyone pass a law, except to reform the Senate. I do ask that Conservatives should have a definite concept of government, that they should endeavour to substitute enlightened administration for hasty lawmaking, an stop the diarrhoea of legislation which now drains parliament of its vitality.
All we are asking for here is for enlightened administration in so far as income tax allowances for university students are concerned. I hope all hon. members read this pamphlet. It contains, as I say, the only coherent statement of Canadian Conservatism I have ever encountered. The case has already been made to the Minister of Finance in connection with medical students, and I think the national federation of Canadian university students has met the medical students' case in this particular regard. I hope that some time in the next year this what is in effect very small concession in terms of revenue for the crown will be granted. I would hope that some of the younger members on the government side who have spoken up rather boldly for increased aid to education would press this point. I know that most hon. members are probably speaking on this matter in caucus, and if they come out into the open and speak on it here it might have some influence on the minister. I do hope these students will get some assistance in this particular field.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to an item which is small in the over-all budget picture but one which is, nevertheless, important to individuals. It has been brought to my notice

by two trade union groups. As the minister knows, if the Minister of National Revenue hopes to collect any income tax from workers. the workers have to receive pay cheques, and there are many workers	who must have tools in order
to earn pay cheques. Take the situation of a journeyman auto mechanic. He has to have tools worth in the neighbourhood of $500-700. A journeyman electrician must possess equipment worth between $300 and $500 and that is a very large outlay for a working man: These people believe, and I also believe, that consideration should be given to allowing the deduction for income tax purposes of the heavy expenditure necessary on tools, and I hope the minister will see if this can be brought about.

The hon. member for Essex East has put on record some reasons which indicate why we are being asked to increase taxation in the manner shown in the resolutions, and to indicate that this increase is not necessitated entirely by considerations of human betterment as the Prime Minister suggested in his broadcast. There is one other reason why an increase in the income tax is required, and that will be apparent on a comparison of the main estimates of 1956-57, the last full year of Liberal administration, with the main estimates of 1959-60. If hon. members are in a position to look at the sheet entitled "Summary of Standard Objects of Expenditures and Special Categories" which was attached to the estimates and then compare it with the similar sheet attached to the estimates for 1959-60, they will find that the item "Interest on Public Debt etc." has increased by $155,500 million, and that is another explanation of why we are being asked to increase the income tax at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If it meets the wishes of the committee I propose to deal now with those points which have been raised before we proceed with the other paragraphs of the resolution under discussion. I think it will meet with the convenience of the house if I deal with the individual points which have been the subjects of questions.
The first point was raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West with regard to the transportation of persons to and from their places of employment. That point was further developed by other hon. members, and the hon. member for Skeena raised the question in particular as applied to loggers.
I think I may say that all the subjects of these individual questions are matters which have been submitted to the department from time to time and which have been carefully

studied by the department. Once in a while, in these debates, some point will arise which is novel, but in the vast majority of cases the points which are, quite properly, raised are matters which have already been submitted to the department for consideration either by hon. members or by interested persons or organizations. I may say in regard to all these matters which have been the subject of questions tonight that they have been studied by the department.
As to requests for further exemptions in particular cases, I simply remind hon. members that in a year when it is found necessary to raise taxes the conditions are hardly appropriate for extending exemptions in individual cases unless those cases are very clear, and I think hon. members will agree that the cases which have been submitted tonight are difficult rather than clear cases. I would say at once that the search for elimination of any discriminatory features in our tax legislature must continue in all circumstances, but while views may differ in regard to some of these individual circumstances, I must say that the type of year we are now facing is certainly not conducive to seeing a clear issue with regard to some of the individual cases which were raised.
As to transportation, in the first place it is very difficult to draw a line. That is a persistent difficulty. One can say in general, or in theory, that if a man lives at a distance from his work the cost of transportation incurred moving to work and back to his home is an expenditure laid out for the purpose of earning his income. But if one examines that situation a little more closely, one finds that this situation applies in a varying degree to practically everyone, and where are we to draw the line? It must be borne in mind, too, that the place of residence is, in the case of most income earners, a matter of choice. One man may choose to live at a distance from his work and he may thereby succeed in lowering his housing costs, but when it is necessary, as it is in tax legislation, to legislate for the generality of cases, the difficulties of trying to introduce exemptions or permit reductions for the purpose of transportation will, I think, be apparent to hon. members, and it will be realized that they present some very thorny problems.
As to the loggers, the hon. member for Skeena acknowledged in his opening remarks that conditions varied in different parts of the country and here again we must legislate for the generality of interest. This is one of the difficulties of any tax legislation; we must always seek to enact rules which are capable of an equitable general application.
As to the loggers, the question was raised, first of all, in reference to transportation. I
Income Tax Act
think I cannot usefully add anything to what I have said already on that matter of transportation. The next point in reference to loggers which was raised by the hon. member for Skeena concerned protective clothing. This has some relationship also to the question of tools which was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Here again, one can theorize and come up with a striking superficial case for an exemption on the ground that a person must have certain types of clothing, or must be equipped with certain tools in order to practise his trade and earn income from so doing. But again I think hon. members will realize on analysis that a thorny difficulty arises over the problem of drawing a line. Everybody owns tools of some kind or another. The people who own tools make use of them. This use may be directly related to earning an income or may be directly related to the saving of expenditure. These tools may be put to a variety of uses. Similarly, in reference to clothing, while it may be possible to theorize about some types of clothing being of a protective nature and not for general use, here again the problem arises as to where to draw the line, because many kinds of what are called protective clothing, whether clothing, shoes or facilities of other kinds, are capable of other uses, either initially or at some stage of their lives. These are just a few of the difficulties one experiences in trying to apply the general rules of taxation to individual cases.
I believe I may lead on from that point to the question that was raised about university students. I may tell the committee that we have received a number of briefs from different groups of university students that do not all ask for the same thing. The hon. member for Trinity read from one brief. We have had other briefs that have submitted requests rather different in scope from the one from which he read.
Let us look in detail at some of these proposals. One was in regard to earnings. We have a problem here, Mr. Chairman. Everybody wishes to see those who are capable of absorbing university education and appreciate it and are prepared to exert themselves for it have the opportunities to obtain that education. In this respect I am simply saying what my predecessors have said on this very subject when it was raised in previous sessions before the change of government. Here I may remind the hon. member for Trinity that he sat on this side of the house supporting a government in which the minister of finance had to face something not unlike what we have had to face in this respect and there were no complaints raised at that time by the hon. member and others of his party when

Income Tax Act
my predecessors in this office were giving reasons why they felt they could not go farther in assisting university students.
Mr. Chairman, the minister would not want to convey the impression that there were no changes made during that period. There were some concessions made by the former minister in his last budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I shall touch on those. When the hon. member asks for further changes let me remind him that further changes were rejected by my predecessors. What is the situation in regard to the earnings of university students? In respect of their earnings they are treated like other persons in this country. A single person may have an exemption of $1,100 if he takes the standard exemption for charitable donations and dues within the scope of the $100 exemption. We have been asked to extend that. I might point out that an extension would mean creating a special class of taxpayer. Under our tax legislation it would mean giving to university students a preferred tax position not enjoyed by anybody else in this country so far as income is concerned. This is a matter that is not to be undertaken lightly.
One must face up to this situation. In the case of young persons leaving high school one may go on to university and another may be obliged to go and work for two or three years to earn enough money to assist him through university. Are we then to say that the person who is not in a financial position that would permit him to proceed immediately to a university education should be taxed as much as anybody else but the person who is in a position of being able to go directly to university should as far as his summer earnings are concerned be in a better position than the man who has to go out and earn a living? Those are weighty and serious considerations.
I have received communications proposing that the parents of university students should have some further exemption not extended to any other class of dependents. Here again hon. members are aware that under the Income Tax Act the parent of a university student is permitted to claim the $500 exemption in respect of that dependent university child while attending university regardless of age.
Here again one must look at the class features of a situation of this kind. One does not wish to create discriminations. Here is a parent of a dependent child who is not able to go to university and yet the law says that in that case that parent shall be entitled to a $500 exemption and no more. Is it to

be regarded as fair and equitable that the child of a father who is in a position to send him to university should thereby enjoy some higher amount of exemption? It has been proposed that this sum should be increased substantially. I think that hon. members on reflection will realize that much as we wish to see every opportunity extended to university students to obtain their education we must be careful as to the methods we choose to assist them lest we thereby create discriminations and advantages that are of a discriminatory nature. That is something against which we must be on our guard.
As to books, one may say again a university student has to have books but then there are lots of other people in the country who have to have books and they are not entitled to income tax exemption for them.
These are some of the difficulties with which we have been confronted especially in a year when we have been obliged to propose increases in the general rates of taxation. I may say that this is not a new problem nor is it one, I am sure, divorced from the personal experience of a good many hon. members in this committee. A large number have had the experience of being university students themselves and know what this problem is and some have also had the experience of being the parents of university students and know what the problems are in that respect.
The tax position in this respect has been advanced. It is now permitted to any dependent to earn $950 in any year before the parent loses the $500 exemption in respect of that dependent. It is true that there are some university students who under present conditions are able to earn more than $950 in a summer and if they do the parent loses the $500 exemption. If they go further and earn $1,100 or more then they become taxable in respect to the excess over the $1,100. I will say with some assurance, however, looking at my friend and classmate of university days, the hon. member for Essex East, that if we had been able in our summers to earn the sums university students are able to earn today we would have considered ourselves very well off. In those days we did not earn more than a fraction of the sums we are discussing today.
But how high were university fees in those days?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is true that university fees have risen. The cost of education and the cost of maintaining a student at university have risen.
You are comparing apples and oranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With respect to some of the deputations I have received from university student groups I may say that I have been told that they regard it as their right to have such tax advantages extended to them as to enable them to complete their university education out of their earnings and not have any indebtedness in respect of their education at the end of it. I find that a little difficult to follow because I believe the experience of those of us here who were university students, certainly in the days when the Leader of the Opposition was our distinguished lecturer, was that there were not many students then who finished their university course without having incurred some debt which they had to work off in the early days of their earning careers.
I am not making any final statement on this subject but I am pointing out the difficulties which are bound to arise when any proposals are made for extending assistance of a special nature to any particular group, and in this case to the university students, however worthy they may be.
One other matter was raised by the hon. member for Cariboo. It was the subject of clearing brush off the land. This, of course, is an aspect of farm improvement. I may say, Mr. Chairman, that in regard to clearing and brushing farm lands the rule is that the clearing of the land of brush, stones, trees and the like is capital expenditure. These are regarded as permanent improvements to the land and it is for that reason that they are not deducted from income as they would be if they were current operating expenses. This is the situation as it applies to the owner of the land.
The situation is somewhat different with respect to the tenant of land who is clearing it. The tenant who makes such expenditures is in a different position because his expenditure is not of a permanent nature, depending upon the particular circumstances of his tenancy and notably the duration of it. These may be expenses deductible in the year made, or they may be amortized over the term of his lease.
I pass now, Mr. Chairman, to some of the remarks of a more general nature. Here we have for I think the third time a resumption of the budget debate in its main aspects. I would not wish to impose upon the committee a repetition of the remarks I made on Tuesday, April 21, in replying to the main opposition amendment to the budget. These matters were all reviewed there. In the speeches made tonight by the hon. member for Essex East and by the Leader of the Opposition we heard and saw the same old straw being threshed. Nothing new was
Income Tax Act
raised by these members tonight. We went over that in the budget debate in the eight days of speeches, half of which came from the opposition, and again this week we have had a resumption of it in a debate on a supply motion; but hon. members opposite seem to think they establish a point by repeating erroneous statements or incomplete statements, and we have heard a good deal of that tonight.
May I first deal with a question that was seriously asked tonight by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, which was his opening subject. It is the question as to whether the tax increases may not result in some increases in the cost of production. Mr. Chairman, here I draw attention again to the places where these increases, these necessary increases, have been imposed. Hon. members opposite talk about a comparison of the reductions which were made in 1957 and again in 1958 with the increases which are proposed in the present budget. In my remarks on April 21 I drew attention to the fact that the reductions which were proposed and brought about in 1957 and 1958 in terms of today's economy, in terms of today's incomes, in terms of today's numbers of taxpayers, are worth to the taxpayers, not the figure that they amounted to when we introduced them but a larger figure. They are worth today an estimated $230 million. The increase in taxes for the present fiscal year amounts to $245 million, but I draw attention to the places where the reductions were made on the one hand, and the places where the increases were made on the other.
The reductions were made for the purpose of benefiting principally the persons in low income brackets. In December, 1957 the proposed increases in the exemptions for dependent children of family allowance age, were from $150 to $250 per annum. For those over family allowance age the increase in exemption was from $400 to $500 per annum. We reduced the rate of tax on the first $1,000 of taxable income by 2 percentage points: we reduced the rate of tax on the second $1,000 of taxable income by one point. That is where the benefit of the reductions was concentrated. In our reductions of tax on business we concentrated on the small corporations. Then, the other reductions we brought about were brought about on smaller estates, on municipalities, on many other persons or enterprises that hon. members will recall from the reductions of 1957 and 1958.
Now, when in the face of the budgetary situation with which we were confronted, we found it necessary to propose taxes we were careful to propose that those taxes be applied where they would hurt least. That is the reason why in the case of the increases in

Income Tax Act
the income tax we have been careful to propose these only with respect to taxable income in excess of $3,000 per annum; that is to say, in the case of the married taxpayer with dependent children, it means that there will not be a cent of additional income tax unless his income is above, in an average case, $6,500.
Now, Mr. Chairman, you will recall that in the budget speech I drew attention to the fact, in a series of illustrations there, that taking the average married person with two dependents, with the decrease in taxes in 1957 and 1958 and the limited increase in 1959, he is better off unless his income is over $7,500 per annum.
In connection with the first paragraph of the resolution for amendment of the Income Tax Act now under discussion, Mr. Chairman, I remind you that the change proposed in this paragraph will have no effect whatever on 3,800,000 of Canada's 4,600,000 income taxpayers. That, I think is, the principal answer to the question of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
It is true that in relation to the proposals we made for augmenting the sources of revenue, the contributions to the old age security fund, the three increases that were proposed of one point on each of the three taxes, personal income tax, corporation tax and sales tax, this does involve an increase of 1 per cent in the tax on the commodities that are subject to the sales tax. But I remind hon. members that this tax was defended by my predecessor, Mr. Abbott, as an eminently fair tax for this purpose.
In these comparisons the minister was making between the reductions in 1957 and the increases now did he include the new 1 per cent levy on incomes for the social security tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, they were included, $2.50 per month.
Does the hon. gentleman say then that for three-quarters of the taxpayers and including the social security levy there is no change this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said they were better off than they were before we came into office back in the dark days when the former government was in office. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River raised a question also about what we see in the press these days concerning certain increases in prices. It may well be that there are increases in prices being announced now on different commodities that are being associated with-
Triggered off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-the increase in the sales tax, but I think that in this regard
tMr. Fleming (Eglinton).]
the hon. member will be fair enough to recognize that the increase in the sales tax warrants an increase of 1 per cent-this is what we are dealing with-as applied to the generality of commodities that are subject to the sales tax, and where increases are being announced these days in excess of that sum, or approximately that proportion, the excess increase is not attributable to the increase in tax.

Will the minister permit a question? Does he realize that in what he is saying he is not being consistent because when he was on this side of the house he pointed out time and again that when there is an increase at the manufacturer's level the retailer applies a percentage mark-up so that the net result to the purchaser is a greater increase than the amount of the increase in the sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is because of that fact that I was careful to add the words I did at the end of my last sentence when I referred to the amount of the tax or that approximate amount. There are mark-ups and that is why I have made allowance for that fact in my answer to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. But some of the increases I have heard of that have gone beyond this figure obviously are not attributable to the increase in the tax at all.
But you started them going.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to the other commodity taxes, I think the hon. gentleman will agree that here it is a matter of personal choice whether-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am very sorry but I have to advise the minister that his time has expired.

I would be glad to ask the
minister a question so that he can go on. The question I would ask is this. Does the minister consider-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I would
assume that the committee is agreeable to the minister continuing.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would much rather hear the question of the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I think I have a right to ask my question because the minister has exhausted his time and I am a member of the house. I am quite willing to give the minister a chance to speak again by asking a question. My question is this. Does the minister consider that these price

increases that were not, as he said, attributable to the tax increase were, in the words of his leader, inexcusable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would consider as inexcusable any attempt to raise a price and attribute the price increase to the increase in tax where it is not in fact attributable to the increase in tax.
You predicted this would happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall endeavour to be brief with regard to some of the other general assertions made here tonight although I do not think the committee expects me to thresh straw again and again that has already been threshed in the course of the last two and a half weeks of debate in this house.
Brevity is not one of your many fine qualities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I could be briefer if hon. members opposite would not go on repeating the same speeches containing the same old errors all the time. I first of all take up the remark of the Leader of the Opposition that the debt this year is going to be in excess of $400 million. He knows the figure is $393 million.
Leaving out social security.
Plus $42 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and the
Leader of the Opposition knows very well how that is being handled and that it is completely in keeping with the way my predecessors have done it in certain years when he was a member of a government that did the very same thing.
How many years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman unhappily has forgotten-
No such thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-some of these things when conditions were comparable, and now that we are moving to put the fund in balance I think he will say, if he will be frank, that this is the proper way to do it and, as I indicated in the budget speech, we will bring the fund into balance within probably the next two and a half years.
Then he talks about the $500 million by way of reductions in expenditures. He had better get his dates straightened out, Mr. Chairman, and be quite frank and forthright with the house with regard to this matter because he has used this figure on several occasions. This goes back to the year 1953 and the general election of that year.

And 1957.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. The leader of the opposition of those days, in going into the election campaign, said that if the people would give him a mandate he would bring about a reduction of $500 million in government taxation, and he showed how it could be done. He said it would be done by a reduction of $200 million in the expenditures of the Department of National Defence and $300 million by eliminating these unplanned surpluses. We were told then by the former government that it could not be done and yet within a matter of a year and a half the reduction in the expenditures of the Department of National Defence had been brought about. The very thing that hon. members opposite said could not be done was done and the fact that they were driven to do it proved that we were right in saying what we did. We were asked about additional payments this year. I dealt with that in detail when I replied in the house on April 21 to the opposition amendment on this subject.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to words of the Prime Minister in a television broadcast recently having to do with expenditures made to meet the recession and asked if some meaning should be read into the words "to meet the recession." Everybody here knows that the increases that have been brought about on the initiative of this government with the support of the house in the various rates of social security payments, old age pensions, old age assistance, pensions for the blind, pensions for the disabled, veterans benefits of numerous kinds, have been written into the statutes of the country, and no one is going to take seriously the suggestion thrown out by the Leader of the Opposition-
It was not a suggestion; it was a quotation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that there is something sinister about such a reference. These increases have been made part of the statute law of this country and I think the Leader of the Opposition will be fair enough to recognize that. As I pointed out in the budget speech of April 9 these payments, which are of a transfer nature, have contributed very greatly to meeting the recession by stimulating consumer purchasing. Even through the recession consumer purchasing was rising and that has been one of the leading elements among the forces that have brought us through the recession and now have planted Canada's feet firmly on the path of recovery.

Could I ask the minister a question? On December 6, 1957, when he introduced these increases, did he use the words "possible recession"?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Possible recession?
Yes, in December, 1957.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my friend asking about the word "possible"?
Or "recession".
There was no recession at that time, according to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were expenditures introduced directly for the purpose of meeting the recession by providing employment. There were increases in these transfer payments, the rates of social security payments, which are designed to assist in meeting problems of persons, principally of very low income, who were the recipients of these pensions. These have greatly assisted in meeting the problem of the recession.
If hon. members opposite are looking for figures, Mr. Chairman, why do they gloss over the figure of $750 million in relation to the housing program? This was a tremendous undertaking through which the government provided funds to assist in the construction of housing in Canada which resulted in the rate of house construction in Canada in 1958 reaching an all-time record.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; the minister has brought into the discussion what I am supposed to have quoted from the Prime Minister's broadcast. He has paraphrased it. I think the exact words should be put on the record so I could not be accused of misrepresenting what the Prime Minister said.
This is the second reference in his broadcast to the purpose of these social security increases, that is to help cure the recession. He said, and I am quoting from the text of the broadcast which the Prime Minister gave. This is the actual text of what the Prime Minister said, and this will appear in the text which I gave to my hon. friend:
These heavy demands for social and individual security measures to meet the recession effects have resulted in a projected deficit for the current year.
This is an accurate quotation on my part, and the deduction I drew from it I think was quite fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let there be no doubt in the mind of anyone about the expression used. My quarrel is with the inference or meaning that the Leader of the Opposition is purporting to read into this statement, which I think is quite unjustified. He was good enough to send me his copy of the text. The Prime Minister, on this page which has been referred to by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East, has been talking about

a great many things. He talks about the big housing program, the $750 million spent on that; he talks about the winter works program; unemployment insurance benefits; human betterment measures; and then he goes on to national health expenditures, welfare and social security payments. He refers to these payments of various kinds about which he has been talking and then he says:
This will bring the total of human betterment payments this year to more than three times the amount of the tax increases. These heavy demands for social and individual security measures to meet the recession effects have resulted in a projected deficit for the current year.
Will my hon. friend permit-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When I was speaking on this subject I drew attention to the fact that we had, even as compared with last year-one does not have to go back to 195657, the last full year of the former government-increased very substantially our expenditures on this social security program and human betterment program.

Will the hon. member permit me to ask him to read that sentence in which the Prime Minister attributes the rise in taxes to the government's program of human betterment; that is the sentence about which we are complaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend has forgotten the sentence in question. Is it the last one, about the deficit? The Prime Minister said:
These heavy demands for social and individual security measures to meet the recession effects have resulted in a projected deficit for the current year.
Is that the sentence?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The other sentence is:
The tax increases in this year's budget are directly related to these human betterment expenditures. In total however, the tax increases are much less than the additional payments to alleviate the effects of the recession.
My hon. friend indicates he would like me to read again the sentence that I just read. It reads:
The tax increases in this year's budget are directly related to these human betterment expenditures.
Of course, they are related to them. We would not have been confronted with this deficit this year if we had not been making these substantially increased expenditures on human betterment, and because our deficit would have been so large this year we felt, in regard to the general inflationary dangers,

it was necessary to budget for a reduction in that deficit. Therefore, we proposed an increase in taxes. The matter is perfectly plain and open for all to see. I am surprised that an acute hon. member like the hon. member for Essex East has somehow or other failed to grasp this. There was a time when the hon. member for Essex East would have grasped the point. He could have done it.
I	can remember the time when he was not nearly so slow about picking up points as he has sought to impress the house tonight that he is. There were days when he was regarded as a person of somewhat acute intelligence. While I realize that perhaps my hon. friend has not applied that acute intelligence of his perhaps as directly to the problem as he should have, and has not devoted as much time and thought to the problem as he might have-
Let us stick to the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -nevertheless, I think we will all have to be a little dubious about the show he put on here of not being able to see through this simple equation.

Would the minister permit
a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

Has the minister forgotten that these social security increases were made in the autumn of 1957, and the Prime Minister did not discover the recession until he read the hidden report in the house on January 20, 1958?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, these increased benefits for the people of Canada were brought into effect on November 15, 1957, and I think the government can claim some credit for moving swiftly to meet the deficiencies left to us by our predecessors in the matter of the social security program. We have no apology to make for having moved swiftly to remedy these deficiencies.
Have you any apology for hiding the eventual bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, we have not hidden the bill and therefore we have no apology to make. I leave that to those who hid reports and other interesting things the people of Canada should have had.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I simply remind hon. members of the vast collection of human betterment measures that the government has sponsored. They are referred to in part
II	of the white paper. The various payments are mentioned, the health grants, hospital construction, health insurance program and
Business of the House
many others. I am sure that these meet with the approval of the majority of the members of this house.

Before the committee rises may I, on behalf of the official opposition, express our appreciation to the minister for his patience this afternoon under difficult circumstances of personal bereavement. I should like to assure him of our sympathy. Perhaps I might repeat that we would have been quite willing to agree to a change in the order of business which would have permitted him to be out of the house today. We greatly appreciate his carrying on in the way he did.

I should like to add to the words used by the Leader of the Opposition the sincere sympathy of the C.C.F. group on learning of the passing of the minister's brother. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, we were quite prepared to go on with some other order of business. I should like to tell the minister, most sincerely, that our thoughts are with him at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do thank the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Assiniboia for their very kind words which, I assure them, I deeply appreciate. I should not have risen at this time to say anything, except that I should like to make a matter of record the kindness that was extended to me this afternoon by both hon. gentlemen in expressing their willingness to have the order of business for the day changed to accommodate the circumstances in which I found myself today. This was a willing and voluntary offer on their part and I am very grateful to them for it. In receiving it I did say to them that I felt the business of the house announced last night should not be disturbed, as I had no wish to impose upon the house.
Progress reported.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could ask the leader of the house if he could indicate the business for tomorrow; and if he could indicate any of the business for next week it would be appreciated.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall commence with the agricultural estimates and then take those of the Department of Labour. I cannot give the house the business for Monday yet. I will try to let hon. members know tomorrow morning.
At ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
